en: The Sutra on the Buddha’s Teaching of the Amitābha Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha,
Who Transcends the Human Realm, Volume One.
Translated by the Layman Zhi Qian of the Yuezhi Nation during the Wu Dynasty.
The Buddha was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain at Rājagṛha.
At that time, there was a great assembly of twelve thousand bhikṣus, all of whom were pure and of one kind, all being arhats:
the Venerable Kauṇḍinya, the Venerable Bāṣpa, the Venerable Mahānāman, the Venerable...
The Venerable Śivaka, the Venerable Pūrṇa, the Venerable Vaimatika, the Venerable Aniruddha,
the Venerable Kātyāyanīputra, the Venerable Uruvilvākāśyapa, the Venerable Nadīkāśyapa,
the Venerable Gayākāśyapa, the Venerable Śāriputra, and the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana.
Furthermore, there were the venerable Mahākāśyapa, the venerable Mahākātyāyana, the venerable Mahākausthila,
the venerable Mahākauṣṭhila, the venerable Mahābrahmāyaṇa,
the venerable Pindolabhāradvāja, the venerable Ānanda, the venerable Nandi, and the venerable Upananda.
The Venerable Pāṭimātṛ, the Venerable Āśvajit, the Venerable Kapphiṇa, the Venerable Mahākoṣṭhila,
the Venerable Mahākātyāyana, the Venerable Vakkula, the Venerable Aniruddha, the Venerable Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra,
the Venerable Cāṣa, and the Venerable Revata— these and other such bhikṣus.
The assembly of monks was exceedingly vast, numbering thousands of billions of people;
they were all bodhisattvas and arhats, infinite and beyond calculation.
They sat together in a great congregation, all of them being worthy ones.

At that time, the Buddha sat in repose, contemplating the Right Path. His face was adorned with light of nine colors, undergoing thousands upon tens of thousands of transformations; the radiance and color were exceedingly bright and great.
Ānanda immediately rose, adjusted his *kāṣāya*, and came forward, prostrating himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet. He then knelt for a long time with palms joined and asked the Buddha:
"Today, the radiance and color of the Buddha’s face undergoes such frequent transformations and becomes so exceedingly bright. Why is this?"
Now the radiance from the Buddha’s face consists of several thousand colors; its brilliance and beauty above and below are such as this.
Since I have served the Buddha, I have never before seen the color of his face as it is today.
"I have never before seen the radiance and majestic power of a Samyaksaṃbuddha to such an extent.
Surely there must be some underlying meaning; I wish to hear it.
The Buddha said:
“Wise Ānanda! Is it that various devas have instructed you, or that the Buddhas have instructed you, that you now question me?
Or do you ask the Buddha out of your own good intention?”
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“No celestial deities have instructed me, nor have any Buddhas taught me to ask the Buddha this.
It was from my own virtuous mind that I understood the Buddha’s intention, and so I asked the Buddha!”

Whenever a Buddha sits, rises, walks, comes, or goes; wherever he intends to go; whatever he is about to do; or whatever instructions he gives—I shall always act in accordance with the Buddha’s intention.

Now, because the Buddha alone contemplates all the Buddhas who have already passed away, all those yet to come, and all the Buddhas currently residing in other Buddha-lands, and because they alone thus contemplate one another in succession, the radiance of the Buddha’s countenance is as it is!
The Buddha said:
"Excellent, excellent,
worthy Ānanda!"
"What you have asked is profoundly deep and most excellent; it will deliver and liberate many.

To ask such a question of the Buddha is superior to making offerings to the Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas throughout a single world-system, or bestowing gifts upon the devas, humans, and even the smallest crawling insects for hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas."
The Buddha said: “Ānanda!
Now you shall deliver and liberate all those in the world of gods, kings, and common people, as well as the species of crawling and flying insects.”
The Buddha said:
"The majestic spiritual power of a Buddha is exceedingly weighty and difficult to withstand.

What you have asked is profoundly deep; that you harbor such a heart of compassion toward the Buddha, and pity for the heavenly kings, emperors, and common people, as well as the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās—this is most excellent. You shall surely cause them all to cross over [to liberation]."
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
“In this world there is the Udumbara tree, which bears fruit but never produces flowers.
Only when a Buddha appears in the world do its flowers bloom!”
"In this world, the appearance of a Buddha is extremely rare to encounter.

Now that I have appeared in the world as a Buddha, if there are those of great virtue, holy wisdom, and a virtuous mind who can anticipate the Buddha's intentions, they shall not serve the Buddha in vain by his side."
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"As for past events that have already transpired since the time of the Mahāsāṃghikas, those kalpas were incalculable and cannot be reckoned."
At that time, there was a past Buddha named Dīpaṃkara.
Next, there was another Buddha named Caṇḍa, who has already passed away.
Next, there was another Buddha named Sumedha Kassapa, who has already passed away.
Next, there was another Buddha named Vimalo, who has already passed away.
Next, there was another Buddha named Ānandari, who has already passed away.
Next, there was another Buddha named Nāgasiri, who has already passed away.
Next, there was another Buddha, named Jāriguptaparākrama, who has already passed away.
Next, there was another Buddha, named Mṛgīkūṭa, who has already passed away.
Next, there was another Buddha named Bhadra, who has already passed away.
Next, there was another Buddha named Cūḍapanthaka, who has already passed away.
Next, there was another Buddha named Vipaśyin, who has already passed away.
Next there was another Buddha named Drāḍhila, who has already passed away.
Next there was another Buddha named Caṇḍa-husita, who has already passed away.
Next, there was another Buddha named Suyāmunasa, who has already passed away.
Next, there was another Buddha named Kaurukullabhadrika, who has already passed away.
Next, there was another Buddha named Śrīghoṣa, who has already passed away.
Next, there was another Buddha named Mahānadi, who has already passed away.
Next, there was another Buddha named Ketusumati, who has already passed away.
Next, there was another Buddha named Rāṣṭrapāla, who has already passed away.
Next there was another Buddha named Yuloujulucai, who has already passed away.
Next there was another Buddha named Manhuquninibobinzhai, who has already passed away.
Next, there was another Buddha named Caṇḍaśubhavasu, who has already passed away.
Next, there was another Buddha named Caṇḍakarabhuja, who has already passed away.
Next there was another Buddha named Pāṇḍubhūminī, who has already passed away.
Next there was another Buddha named Bhavasvāti, who has already passed away.
Next there was another Buddha named Aśvita-kevalin, who has already passed away.
Next there was another Buddha named Vāsudeva, who has already passed away.
Next, there was another Buddha named Citta, who has already passed away.
Next, there was another Buddha named Dharmavardhana, who has already passed away.
Next, there was another Buddha named Śreyas, who has already passed away.
Next, there was another Buddha named Luyeda, who has already passed away.
Next, there was another Buddha named Sengjialomiloujiada, who has already passed away.
Next, there was another Buddha named Dāmodarāvinandan, who has already passed away.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“Next, there was another Buddha named Lohityagotra, who taught in the world; his lifespan was forty-two kalpas.”
At that time, there was a great king of a world-empire who, upon hearing the Buddha’s sutras and the Way, felt immediate joy and attained understanding;
he then renounced his kingdom and abdicated his throne to become a śramaṇa, named Dharmaka.
Practicing the path of a bodhisattva, he was a man of eminent talent, possessing wisdom and valor that far surpassed those of ordinary people.
He went to the place where the Buddha Luyi Xunluo was staying, prostrated before the Buddha, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"I wish to seek Buddhahood through the path of a bodhisattva, so that when I later become a Buddha, among the countless Buddhas of the eight directions and the zenith and nadir, my wisdom and valor shall be the most supreme."
The radiance from my head shall be like the radiance of a Buddha, its blazing light illuminating infinitely.
The land where I dwell shall be composed of the seven treasures, naturally and exceedingly soft and beautiful.

When I later become a Buddha, may the name by which I am taught be heard throughout the eight directions and the zenith and nadir across incalculable Buddha-lands, such that there is no one who does not hear and know my name.

All the countless devas and humans, as well as the various classes of crawling and flying insects, who come to be born in my land, shall all become bodhisattvas and arhats; my land shall be infinitely superior to all other buddha-fields.
"Can such a thing as this be attained?
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"The Buddha Lohitya, knowing that the aspirations of the noble and wise one were swift and virtuous, immediately preached a sutra for the Bodhisattva Dharmaka, saying:"

"For example, if a single person were to measure the waters of the great ocean with a peck-measure, continuing for an entire kalpa without ceasing, they might still exhaust it until it is empty and reach its bottom mud."
If a person seeks the Way with a sincere heart, how could it be that they should not attain it?
If one seeks and strives without ceasing, one will surely obtain whatever one desires in one's heart.
When the Bodhisattva Dharmaka heard the Buddha Luyi Xunla preach the sutra in this manner, he was immediately filled with great joy and leaped for gladness.

That Buddha then selected from among two hundred and ten billion buddha-lands the virtues and faults of the devas and people, as well as the excellence and flaws of those lands, according to what the Bodhisattva desired and wished for in his heart.

When the Buddha Yigengluo had finished preaching this sutra, Damojia immediately unified his mind and attained the divine eye of penetrating vision; he saw for himself the good and evil of the gods and people, as well as the beauty and ugliness of the lands, within two hundred and ten billion Buddha-fields.

Thereupon, selecting that which was wished for in his heart, he obtained this Sūtra of the Twenty-four Vows; he then practiced it, seeking it with diligent effort, heroic vigor, and arduous perseverance.
Thus, throughout incalculable kalpas, he served and made offerings to innumerable past Buddhas.

Subsequently, that Bodhisattva Dharmākara attained Buddhahood for himself; his name is Amitābha Buddha. His supreme wisdom, courage, and radiance are peerless, and the land where he currently resides is exceedingly delightful and excellent.

In other Buddha-fields throughout the ten directions—above and below—he instructs the countless devas, humans, and all classes of beings, from those that fly and crawl to those that wriggle, so that none fail to attain transcendence and liberation from sorrow and suffering.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:

“When Amitābha Buddha was a bodhisattva, he constantly practiced these twenty-four vows. He treasured and cherished them, maintaining them with reverence and caution; through diligent meditation, he surpassed all others, standing out preeminently and uniquely, such that none could equal him.”
The Buddha said:
"What are the twenty-four vows?
The first vow:..."
"When I become a Buddha, may there be no hells, animals, hungry ghosts, or any crawling and flying insects within my land.
Only upon obtaining this vow shall I become a Buddha; if I do not obtain this vow, I shall never become a Buddha."
"The second vow:
When I attain Buddhahood, may there be no women in my land; if any woman wishes to be reborn in my land, she shall immediately become a man.

May all the countless devas, humans, and even the smallest crawling insects who come to be reborn in my land be born by transformation within lotus flowers in ponds of the seven treasures. Upon reaching maturity, they shall all become bodhisattvas and arhats in infinite numbers."
"If I attain these vows, I shall become a Buddha; if I do not attain these vows, I shall never become a Buddha. 'Third Vow:
When I become a Buddha, may my land be composed of the seven treasures, naturally appearing, vast, expansive, boundless, and exceedingly soft and beautiful.'"
The dwellings, garments, and food they inhabit shall all be spontaneous, exactly like the abodes of the sixth heavenly king.
Only upon obtaining these vows will he become a Buddha; as long as he does not obtain these vows, he shall never become a Buddha.
"The fourth vow:
When I become a Buddha, may my name be heard throughout the eight directions and the zenith and nadir across incalculable Buddha-lands.
May all Buddhas, each within the great assemblies of their bhikṣu saṃghas, proclaim the excellence of my merits and my land."
May all devas, humans, and even the smallest crawling insects who hear my name be filled with a heart of compassion and leap for joy; may they all be reborn in my land.
"Only upon obtaining these vows shall I become a Buddha; if I do not obtain these vows, I shall never become a Buddha.
'The fifth vow:

When I become a Buddha, may all the countless devas and humans of the eight directions and the zenith and nadir, as well as the wriggling and crawling creatures—if they have committed evil in previous lives—upon hearing my name and desiring to be reborn in my land, immediately reform themselves and repent their transgressions, practice the Way and perform good deeds, uphold the sutras and precepts, and aspire to be reborn in my land without ceasing.'"
At the end of their lives, they shall all be prevented from returning to the realms of hell-beings, animals, or hungry ghosts, and shall instead be born in my land according to their wishes.
Only upon obtaining this vow shall one become a Buddha; as long as this vow is not obtained, one shall never become a Buddha.
"The sixth vow:

When I attain Buddhahood, may the gods and people of the countless Buddha-lands in the eight directions and above and below—whether they be good men or good women—who, for my sake, perform further acts of merit such as practicing charity, circumambulating stupas, burning incense, scattering flowers, lighting lamps, hanging various silk banners, providing food to śramaṇas, erecting stupas, building monasteries, and severing craving and desire, and who wish to be reborn in my land, shall be reborn there as bodhisattvas."
"Only upon obtaining these vows shall I become a Buddha; if I do not obtain these vows, I shall never become a Buddha.
'The Seventh Vow:

When I become a Buddha, may the countless Buddha-lands of the eight directions and the zenith and nadir—wherever there are devas and humans, or good sons and good daughters who practice the path of a Bodhisattva and uphold the Sūtras of the Six Pāramitās [be so transformed]."

If one becomes a śramaṇa, does not violate the sūtras or precepts, severs craving and desire, maintains the purity of the fast and the precepts, and single-mindedly contemplates being born in my land without ceasing day or night; [then he shall be reborn there].
When that person’s life is about to end, I shall immediately fly with the bodhisattvas and arhats to welcome them;
they will then be reborn in my land, becoming an avaivartika bodhisattva of courageous wisdom.
"Only upon obtaining these vows shall I become a Buddha; if I do not obtain these vows, I shall never become a Buddha.
'The eighth vow:

When I become a Buddha, may all the bodhisattvas in my land who wish to be born in other buddha-lands of the ten directions never again fall into the hells, the realm of birds and beasts, or the realm of hungry ghosts (preta), and may they all attain the Way of the Buddha.'"
"Only upon attaining these vows shall I become a Buddha; if I do not attain these vows, I shall never become a Buddha.
'The ninth vow:

When I become a Buddha, may all the bodhisattvas and arhats in my land have countenances that are perfectly upright, pure, and beautiful, all of one color and of one kind, just like the devas of the sixth heaven.'"
Only upon attaining these vows shall I become a Buddha; if I do not attain these vows, I shall never become a Buddha.
"The tenth vow:
When I become a Buddha, may all the bodhisattvas and arhats in my land be of one mind in their thoughts and desires, such that they mutually understand each other's intentions even before speaking."
"Only when this vow is fulfilled shall I become a Buddha; if this vow is not attained, I shall never become a Buddha.
'The eleventh vow:
When I become a Buddha, may all the bodhisattvas and arhats in my land be entirely free from any lustful or licentious thoughts.'"
He shall never again harbor thoughts of women, nor shall he ever possess anger or delusion.
Only upon obtaining these vows shall he become a Buddha; without obtaining these vows, he shall never become a Buddha.
"The twelfth vow:
When I attain Buddhahood, may all the bodhisattvas and arhats in my land have hearts that respect and love one another, and never harbor feelings of jealousy or hatred toward each other."
"Only upon obtaining these vows shall I become a Buddha; if I do not obtain these vows, I shall never become a Buddha.
'The thirteenth vow:

When I become a Buddha, may all the bodhisattvas in my land who wish to collectively make offerings to the innumerable Buddhas of the eight directions, above, and below, be able to fly there at will. Should they desire any of the ten thousand kinds of natural objects, may they all appear before them immediately, so that they may take them to offer to the Buddhas.'"
After they have all been reached, before the sun has reached its zenith, he shall immediately fly back to his own country.
Only upon obtaining this vow will he become a Buddha; if he does not obtain this vow, he shall never become a Buddha.
"The fourteenth vow:

When I attain Buddhahood, whenever the bodhisattvas and arhats in my land wish to eat, there shall spontaneously appear in their bowls made of the seven treasures a hundred-flavored meal before them; once they have finished eating, it shall vanish of its own accord."
"Only upon obtaining these vows shall I become a Buddha; without obtaining these vows, I shall never become a Buddha.
'The fifteenth vow:

When I become a Buddha, may all the bodhisattvas in my land have bodies the color of purple-polished gold, possessing the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, all exactly like those of a Buddha.'"
"Only upon obtaining this vow shall I become a Buddha; if I do not obtain this vow, I shall never become a Buddha.
'The sixteenth vow:

When I become a Buddha, may all the bodhisattvas and arhats in my land have voices like the sound of three hundred bells, and may their preaching of the sutras and their practice of the Way be identical to those of a Buddha.'"
"Only upon attaining these vows shall I become a Buddha; if I do not attain these vows, I shall never become a Buddha.
'The seventeenth vow:
When I become a Buddha, may I possess clear vision and penetrating hearing, and may my power of flight be ten times greater than that of all other Buddhas.'"
"Only upon attaining these vows shall I become a Buddha; if I do not attain these vows, I shall never become a Buddha.
'The Eighteenth Vow:
When I become a Buddha, may my wisdom in preaching the sutras and practicing the Way be ten times greater than that of all other Buddhas.'"
"Only upon obtaining these vows shall I become a Buddha; if I do not obtain these vows, I shall never become a Buddha.
"The nineteenth vow:

When I become a Buddha, may all the gods, humans, and even the smallest crawling and flying insects throughout the countless Buddha-lands of the eight directions and the zenith and nadir, all attain the human path and become Pratyekabuddhas or Arhats. May they all sit in meditation with single-minded focus and, together, attempt to calculate and know the number of my lifespan in thousands of billions of kalpas, yet ensure that none are able to fully know the extent of my life."
"Only upon obtaining this vow shall I become a Buddha; if I do not obtain this vow, I shall never become a Buddha. "The twentieth vow:

When I become a Buddha, may all the devas, humans, and even the smallest crawling insects within a thousand billion Buddha-lands in the eight directions and above and below, all become Pratyekabuddhas and Arhats. May they all sit in meditation with single-minded focus, desiring to calculate the number of Bodhisattvas and Arhats in my land—how many thousands of billions of people there are—and yet may there be none at all who is able to know that number."
"Only upon obtaining these vows shall I become a Buddha; if I do not obtain these vows, I shall never become a Buddha.
'The twenty-first vow: When I become a Buddha, may the lifespan of all the bodhisattvas and arhats in my land be incalculable kalpas.'"
"Only upon obtaining this vow shall I become a Buddha; if I do not obtain this vow, I shall never become a Buddha.
"The twenty-second vow:

When I become a Buddha, may all the Bodhisattvas and Arhats in my land possess wisdom and valor, such that they know their own past lives throughout hundreds of millions of kalpas. May they retroactively know their infinite deeds of good and evil, seeing through all things with penetrating clarity, and know all matters of the ten directions—past, future, and present."
"Only upon attaining this vow shall I become a Buddha; if I do not attain this vow, I shall never become a Buddha.
'The twenty-third vow:
When I become a Buddha, may all the bodhisattvas and arhats in my land possess wisdom and valor, and may there be radiance upon the crowns of their heads.'"
"Only upon obtaining this vow shall I become a Buddha; if I do not obtain this vow, I shall never become a Buddha.
'The twenty-fourth vow:

When I become a Buddha, may the light from the crown of my head be exceedingly beautiful, surpassing the brilliance of the sun and moon by hundreds of thousands of millions of times, and excelling that of all other Buddhas.'"
The flames of my radiance shall illuminate countless worlds beneath heaven; all places of darkness shall become brilliantly bright.
May all gods, humans, and even the smallest crawling insects who, upon seeing my light, give rise to a heart of compassion and perform good deeds, be reborn in my land.
"Only upon attaining these vows shall he become a Buddha; if he does not attain these vows, he shall never become a Buddha.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"When Amitābha was a bodhisattva, he constantly practiced and upheld these twenty-four vows."
They practice the giving of alms and do not violate the prohibitions of the Path; they cultivate patience, diligence, single-mindedness, and wisdom;
their aspirations are always courageous and resolute, and they do not disparage the sutras or the Dharma.

Seeking without ceasing, he repeatedly and alone renounced his kingdom and abdicated his kingship, severing all ties to wealth and sensual pleasure. With clarity and vigor, he pursued his vows without partiality toward friend or foe; accumulating merit and virtue over incalculable kalpas, he has now attained Buddhahood by himself, having fully realized all these goals without losing a single fraction of his effort.
The Buddha said:
“The radiance of Amitābha Buddha is most honored, foremost, and beyond compare;
the radiances of all other Buddhas cannot equal it.”
Among the countless Buddhas of the eight directions, above, and below, there are Buddhas whose light from the crown of their heads illuminates seven *zhang*,
some whose light from the crown of their heads illuminates one *li*, some whose light from the crown of their heads illuminates two *li*,
some whose light from the crown of their heads illuminates five *li*, and some whose light from the crown of their heads illuminates ten [li].
In some, the light from the crown of the Buddha’s head illuminates twenty *li*; in some, the light from the crown of the Buddha’s head illuminates forty *li*;
in some, the light from the crown of the Buddha’s head illuminates eighty *li*; in some, the light from the crown of the Buddha’s head illuminates one hundred and sixty *li*;
and in some, the light from the crown of the Buddha’s head illuminates three hundred and twenty *li*.
There is a Buddha whose light from the crown of his head illuminates six hundred and forty *li*;

there is a Buddha whose light from the crown of his head illuminates one thousand three hundred *li*; there is a Buddha whose light from the crown of his head illuminates two thousand six hundred *li*;

there is a Buddha whose light from the crown of his head illuminates five thousand two hundred *li*; and there is a Buddha whose light from the crown of his head illuminates ten thousand four hundred *li*.
In one hundred *li*, there is a Buddha whose crown-light illuminates twenty-one thousand *li*;
there is a Buddha whose crown-light illuminates forty-two thousand *li*; there is a Buddha whose crown-light illuminates eighty-four thousand *li*;
there is a Buddha whose crown-light illuminates one hundred seventy thousand *li*; and there is a Buddha whose crown-light...
The light from the uṣṇīṣa of one Buddha illuminates three hundred and fifty thousand *li*; the light from the uṣṇīṣa of another Buddha illuminates seven hundred thousand *li*;
the light from the uṣṇīṣa of another Buddha illuminates one million five hundred thousand *li*;
the light from the uṣṇīṣa of another Buddha illuminates three million *li*; and the light from the uṣṇīṣa of another Buddha illuminates six million *li*.
There are Buddhas whose light from the crown of their heads illuminates one Buddha-field; there are Buddhas whose light from the crown of their heads illuminates two Buddha-fields;
there are Buddhas whose light from the crown of their heads illuminates four Buddha-fields; there are Buddhas whose light from the crown of their heads illuminates eight Buddha-fields;
there are Buddhas whose light from the crown of their heads illuminates fifteen Buddha-fields; and there are Buddhas whose light from the crown of their heads...
The radiance of some illuminates thirty buddha-fields; the radiance from the crown of the head of some buddhas illuminates sixty buddha-fields;
the radiance from the crown of the head of some buddhas illuminates one hundred and twenty buddha-fields;

the radiance from the crown of the head of some buddhas illuminates two hundred and forty buddha-fields; the radiance from the crown of the head of some buddhas illuminates five hundred buddha-fields. There are...

There are those whose radiance from the crown of the Buddha’s head illuminates a thousand buddha-fields; there are those whose radiance from the crown of the Buddha’s head illuminates two thousand buddha-fields;

there are those whose radiance from the crown of the Buddha’s head illuminates four thousand buddha-fields; there are those whose radiance from the crown of the Buddha’s head illuminates eight thousand buddha-fields;
there are those whose radiance from the crown of the Buddha’s head illuminates sixteen thousand buddha-fields; and there are...
The light from the uṣṇīṣa of some Buddhas illuminates thirty-two thousand Buddha-fields;
the light from the uṣṇīṣa of others illuminates sixty-four thousand Buddha-fields; the light from the uṣṇīṣa of others illuminates one hundred and thirty thousand Buddha-fields;
the light from the uṣṇīṣa of others illuminates two hundred and sixty thousand Buddha-fields; and the light from the uṣṇīṣa of yet others...
Some illuminate five hundred thousand buddha-fields; some have light from the crowns of their heads that illuminates one million buddha-fields;
and some have light from the crowns of their heads that illuminates two million buddha-fields.
The Buddha said:
"The blazing radiance from the crowns of the heads of the countless Buddhas of the eight directions, above, and below, all shines in this same manner.
The blazing radiance from the crown of Amitābha Buddha’s head shines upon ten million buddha-lands."
Why is it that the radiance of the Buddhas has varying ranges of illumination?
It is because when they were seeking the Way in their past lives as bodhisattvas, the merits resulting from their respective vows differed in magnitude;
when they subsequently attained Buddhahood, each obtained the fruit of those vows, and thus their radiance differs accordingly.
The majestic spiritual power of all Buddhas is equal; acting according to their sovereign will, they perform deeds without prior calculation.
Among them, the light of Amitābha Buddha is the greatest, such that the lights of all other Buddhas cannot reach its extent.
The Buddha praised him, saying:
"The light of Amitābha Buddha is most excellent!
The light of Amitābha Buddha is most excellent!"
Within the realm of goodness, it is luminous and excellent; it is exceedingly delightful beyond compare, transcendent and infinite.
The radiance of Amitābha Buddha is pure and stainless, without any deficiency or diminution.
The radiance of Amitābha Buddha is exquisite and surpasses the brilliance of the sun and moon by hundreds of thousands of millions of times.

It is the ultimate brightness among the radiances of all Buddhas, the ultimate excellence among radiances, the ultimate majesty among radiances, and the ultimate goodness among radiances. He is the king among all Buddhas, the most venerable among radiances, and the supreme, boundless luminosity among radiances.
Its flames illuminate countless worlds below; even in the most obscure and dark places, there is always great radiance.

Among all people and the various classes of creatures, both flying and crawling, there are none who do not behold the light of Amitābha Buddha; and among those who behold it, there are none who do not feel a heart of compassion and joy.
Among those in the world who are lustful, wrathful, or deluded, none fail to perform wholesome deeds upon seeing the light of Amitābha Buddha.

Those dwelling in the hells, among birds and beasts, or as hungry ghosts—in places of interrogation, scourging, and diligent suffering—all cease their torment when the light of Amitābha Buddha reaches them; thereafter, there is none who does not attain liberation from sorrow and pain after death.

The radiance of Amitābha Buddha’s fame resounds throughout the eight directions, above and below, without end or limit; there are countless Buddha-lands where all devas and humans have not failed to hear and know of it, and among those who have heard and known it, there are none who are not delivered and liberated.
The Buddha said,
"It is not only I who praise the radiance of Amitābha Buddha.
In the eight directions and above and below, countless Buddhas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and arhats all praise him in this same way."
The Buddha said:
"If there are people—whether good men or good women—who hear the name of Amitābha Buddha and praise his radiance."

Morning and evening, they constantly praise its radiant beauty with an uninterrupted and sincere heart; according to their aspiration, they shall be reborn in the land of Amitābha Buddha and attain the respect of the multitude of bodhisattvas and arhats.
If he later becomes a Buddha, his radiance shall likewise be praised in such a manner by the countless Buddhas, Pratyekabuddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Arhats of the eight directions, above, and below.

Thereupon, the assembly of bhikṣus, the bodhisattvas, the arhats, the devas, the kings, and the people, upon hearing this, were all filled with joy and leaped for gladness; there was none who did not offer praise.
The Buddha said:

"I have described the radiance of Amitābha Buddha as magnificent and sublime, its praise as swift and virtuous; even if one were to speak for a single kalpa day and night, one would not yet have finished.
I have merely told you this brief account."

When the Buddha spoke of Amitābha Buddha as a bodhisattva seeking and attaining these twenty-four vows, Prince Ajātaśatru, together with five hundred sons of elders (gṛhapati), each holding a golden flowered parasol, arrived together at the place where the Buddha was. They came forward to pay homage to the Buddha, touching their heads and faces to the Buddha’s feet. Having all offered their golden flowered parasols before the Buddha, they withdrew and sat to one side to listen to the sutra.

When Prince Ajātaśatru and five hundred sons of elders heard the twenty-four vows of Amitābha Buddha, they were all filled with great joy and leaped for gladness; in their hearts, they made this vow together:
"When we later become Buddhas, may we all be just like Amitābha Buddha."
The Buddha, knowing this immediately, addressed the assembly of bhikṣus:
"This Crown Prince Ajātaśatru and these five hundred sons of elders shall, after incalculable kalpas, all become buddhas just like Amitābha Buddha."
The Buddha said:

"This Crown Prince Ajātaśatru and the five hundred sons of elders have dwelled in the bodhisattva path for incalculable kalpas; having each made offerings to four hundred billion buddhas, they have now come once more to make offerings to me."

The Crown Prince Ajātaśatru and these five hundred sons of elders were all my disciples during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha in a previous life; it is now that they have once again gathered together and encountered one another.
When the monks heard these words of the Buddha, they all leaped for joy, and there was none among them who did not rejoice on his behalf.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Since Amitābha attained Buddhahood, ten minor kalpas have passed."
The land where he dwells is named Sumati; it lies directly to the west, a distance of ten trillion *sumeru* mountains from the boundaries of this Jambudvīpa Buddha-field.

The ground of that land is composed entirely of natural seven treasures: the first treasure is white silver, the second is gold, the third is crystal, the fourth is lapis lazuli, the fifth is coral, the sixth is amber, and the seventh is musaragalva; these constitute the seven treasures.
All take themselves together as their ground; it is vast, expansive, and infinitely great.
They all intermingle with one another, turning into one another’s midst, each brilliantly radiant and mutually illuminating, exceedingly soft and beautiful, most exquisite beyond compare.

That ground of the seven treasures is formed by the natural convergence of the finest essences from all the various treasures of the eight directions, above, and below; it is merely a product of transformation.
These treasures are all comparable to the seven treasures of the sixth heaven.
In that land there is no Mount Sumeru; its sun, moon, stars, and planets, as well as the first and second heavens—the Cāturmahārājika and the Trāyastriṃśa—reside entirely within the void of space.
In that land there is no great ocean, nor is there any small sea; there are no rivers, streams, or the Ganges.
There are no mountains, forests, or valleys, nor is there any place of darkness or obscurity; the ground of the seven treasures throughout that land is entirely level and even.
There are no beings in the hells, among animals, or as hungry ghosts, nor any that fly or crawl.
There are no asuras, nāgas, or spirits.

There is never a time of rain from heaven, nor are there spring, summer, autumn, or winter; there is neither great cold nor great heat, but it is always temperate, moderate, and perfectly pleasant, being incomparably delightful and excellent.

There were naturally present all manner of things and foods of a hundred flavors; whatever one desired to obtain would spontaneously appear before them, and whatever was not needed would spontaneously vanish.
For example, like the natural objects on the sixth heaven, they are as spontaneous as nature itself and all accord with one's wishes.
In that land, there are exclusively bodhisattvas and arhats; there are no women, and their lifespan lasts for incalculable kalpas.
When women were reborn there, they immediately transformed into men.
There were immeasurable numbers of bodhisattvas and arhats, all of whom possessed the power of clairvoyance and clairaudience;
they could see one another from afar, gaze upon one another from afar, and hear one another’s voices from afar.
All those who seek the Way and are virtuous are of one and the same kind; there are no others who differ from them.
Those bodhisattvas and arhats all have countenances that are upright and handsome, pure and exceptionally beautiful, and they are all of one uniform color, with none being at all ugly or deformed.

All these bodhisattvas and arhats are courageous and possess sharp wisdom; all wear robes that appear spontaneously. Whatever moral principles they contemplate in their minds, and whatever they wish to speak, others already know their thoughts in advance.
Their speech always concerns upright matters, and whenever they speak, they invariably discourse upon the sutras and the Way, never speaking of other evils.
Their speech and resonance were like the sound of three hundred bells.
They all respected and loved one another, with none who harbored jealousy or hatred; they always addressed one another according to their age, seniority, rank, and order of precedence.
Acting with righteousness as one does with ritual propriety, they treat one another with mutual respect and service, like elder and younger brothers.
Treading upon righteousness through benevolence, they do not engage in reckless actions or speech.
Admonishing and instructing one another, they ensure that they do not act in opposition or contravention, but rather receive and uphold one another's teachings.
Their minds were all pure and clean, free from greed or longing; they never harbored thoughts of anger, lust, or debauchery, nor did they exhibit any signs of folly or delusion.
They had no perverse thoughts or intentions toward women; instead, they were all possessed of wisdom and vigor, with harmonious hearts that delighted in and took joy in the Way of the sutras.
They know for themselves the origins from which they came in the past, spanning billions of kalpas, including their past lives, virtues and evils, and their survival or demise;
they also retroactively know the infinite present.

"The lecture halls and monasteries taught by Amitābha Buddha are all spontaneously composed of the seven treasures—gold, silver, crystal, lapis lazuli, white jade, amber, and musaragalva—which are formed together with one another, exceedingly beautiful and radiant, surpassingly exquisite beyond compare."
Furthermore, there is no creator, for it is unknown from whence it comes; nor is there anyone who brings it here, nor is there any place to which it goes.

Because the vows and virtues of Amitābha Buddha are profound, and because that person has performed wholesome deeds, according to the meaning of the sutras and the discourse therein—preaching the sutras, practicing the Way, and participating in assemblies within that realm—they are naturally born through transformation.

Their lecture halls and monasteries were further adorned with towers and railings made of the seven treasures, and were decorated with necklaces fashioned from gold, silver, crystal, lapis lazuli, white jade, amber, and musaragalva;
furthermore, canopies of white pearls, moon-pearls, and maṇi-jewels covered them above.
They all produced the five musical notes themselves, which were incomparably beautiful.

The dwellings where the bodhisattvas and arhats resided were likewise fashioned from the seven treasures—gold, silver, crystal, lapis lazuli, coral, amber, musaragalva, and agate—which combined together to form their respective abodes.
Each of these had seven-jeweled towers and pavilions with railings, further adorned with necklaces made of gold, silver, crystal, lapis lazuli,
white jade, amber, and musaragalva; furthermore, they were covered above by canopies of white pearls, moon-pearls, and maṇi jewels,
all of which produced their own five kinds of musical sounds.

“In the lecture halls and monasteries of Amitābha Buddha, as well as within the residences where the various bodhisattvas and arhats dwell, there are everywhere, both inside and out, natural flowing springs and bathing pools. These all arise spontaneously together with the seven treasures—gold, silver, crystal, lapis lazuli, amber, and musaragalva—which combine and mutually form one another.”
The Lake of Pure Gold has sand at its bottom of white silver;
the Lake of Pure White Silver has sand at its bottom of yellow gold;
the Lake of Pure Crystal has sand at its bottom of lapis lazuli.
In the pure lapis lazuli pond, the sand at the bottom of the water is crystal.
In the pure coral pond, the sand at the bottom of the water is amber.
In the pure amber pond, the sand at the bottom of the water is coral.
In the pool of pure musaragalva, the sand on the bottom is agate.
In the pool of pure agate, the sand on the bottom is musaragalva.
In the pool of pure white jade, the sand on the bottom is purple-gold.
As for the pool of pure purple-gold, the sand at its bottom is white jade.
Furthermore, there are two other pools formed by two precious substances together; the sand at their bottoms is gold and silver.
Furthermore, among them, there are some ponds made of three kinds of jewels together; the sand at their bottom consists of gold, silver, and crystal.
Furthermore, among them, there are some ponds made of four kinds of jewels together; the sand at their bottom consists of gold, silver, crystal, and lapis lazuli.
Among them, there are some ponds made from five kinds of jewels together; the sand at their bottom consists of gold, silver, crystal, lapis lazuli, and coral.
Among them, there are some ponds made from six kinds of jewels together; the sand at their bottom consists of gold, silver, crystal, lapis lazuli, coral, and amber.
Among them, there are some ponds formed by seven precious substances combined together; the sands at their bottom consist of gold, silver, crystal, lapis lazuli, coral, amber, and musaragalva.

Among them are bathing pools forty *li* long, some eighty *li* long, some one hundred and sixty *li* long, some three hundred and twenty *li* long, some six hundred and forty *li* long, some one thousand two hundred and eighty *li* long, some two thousand five hundred and sixty *li* long, some five thousand one hundred and twenty *li* long, some ten thousand two hundred and forty *li* long, and some twenty thousand four hundred and eighty *li* long.
That pond is exactly equal in length and breadth; it is a bathing pool constantly used by all the bodhisattvas and arhats.
The Buddha said:
“The bathing pool of Amitābha Buddha is forty-eight thousand li in length and also forty-eight thousand li in breadth; that pool is entirely composed of the seven treasures joined together.”
The sand at the bottom of that water consists of white pearls, moon-pearls, and maṇi-jewels.
The water in the bathing pools of Amitābha Buddha, as well as the bodhisattvas and arhats, is all fragrant, pure, and clean.
Within the ponds there are fragrant flowers, all of which grow spontaneously in a hundred varieties, each of diverse colors;
these flowers of various hues and fragrances have branches with a thousand petals, their exquisite scent being beyond compare and indescribable.
These flowers are neither flowers of the mundane world nor flowers of the heavens;
their fragrance pervades the eight directions, above and below, being the essence among all floral scents, produced spontaneously through transformation.
The water in that pond flows and circulates, pouring from one place to another;
as it flows, it is neither sluggish nor rapid, and it produces the sounds of the five musical notes.
The Buddha said:

"In the innumerable Buddha-lands of the eight directions, above, and below—including all devas, humans, and even the crawling and wriggling creatures—those who are born in the land of Amitābha Buddha are all born by transformation within lotus flowers in ponds of the seven treasures, where they immediately grow to full size naturally.
There is no one to nurse them, and they all partake of natural food."

Their bodies are neither the bodies of worldly humans nor the bodies of celestial beings; they are all accumulations of the virtue of manifold good deeds, having entirely received natural, void-like bodies and infinite forms that are exceedingly beautiful beyond compare.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"Suppose a poor beggar from the world were made to dwell beside a sovereign emperor; would his facial features, shape, and complexion resemble those of the emperor?"
Ānanda said:
"If a prince were to dwell beside a sovereign king, his facial features and appearance would be exceedingly ugly and unpleasing;
he would not equal the king by even a hundred thousand ten-millionth part."
Why is this? Because the beggar is impoverished and at the height of misery; his food and drink are always coarse, and he never enjoys fine meals.

Since his food is poor, he cannot eat his fill; his food merely sustains life, with his bones and joints propping each other up. Having no means to provide for himself, he is constantly destitute and possesses no store.
They suffer from hunger and cold, trembling with anxiety and grief.

This is solely because in their past lives they were foolish and ignorant, lacking wisdom and being stingy and greedy; they refused to practice compassion or perform good deeds with broad love and generosity.

They desired only to obtain things for nothing, coveting food and drink to eat alone and indulge in delicacies. They did not believe that giving and lending would result in rewards later, nor did they believe that performing good deeds would bring blessings in future lives. Thus, they remained dull-witted and obstinate, further committing all manner of evils.

Thus, when his life ends and his wealth is exhausted, having been naturally devoid of kindness and virtue and possessing nothing to rely upon, he enters the evil realms where he sits amidst constant suffering; only then can he emerge and attain liberation.
Having been born as a human in this life, he was made lowly, becoming the son of a poor household.

His physical form was coarse and his appearance extremely ugly; his clothing was tattered and worn out, and he stood alone and destitute, unable even to cover his body, surviving only by begging for alms.

Starving, cold, and suffering, their faces were emaciated and wretched, unlike those of human beings; because they had committed such deeds in their previous lives, they now endured these calamities and punishments. When the multitude saw them, none felt any compassion.
Cast aside from the ways of the marketplace, exposed to the elements, emaciated by illness, black and hideous to an extreme—such that he is not even equal to other men.
"What is it, then, that makes the sovereign among men uniquely honored and most excellent?"

In all these cases, when they were human beings in previous lives, they performed good deeds and faithfully accepted the Way of the scriptures; they distributed bounty and bestowed virtue, practiced universal love and conformed to righteousness, were compassionate and benevolent, delighted in giving, and were not greedy for food and drink, sharing them with the multitude.

Without any sense of lack or stinginess, and entirely free from conflict or contention, he attained virtuous blessings; at the end of his life, his merit followed him, and he did not fall into the evil realms.
Now born as a human, he was born into a royal family, naturally noble and uniquely sovereign as a ruler, governing the people and acting as their preeminent leader.

His face and features are pure white, his countenance is serene and pleasing, and his body is upright, such that all revere and serve him. He enjoys fine food and exquisite clothing as he desires, according to his heart's content.

Whatever he delights in appears before him spontaneously, without any opposition or contention. Among humans, he is exceptionally handsome; free from sorrow and full of joy, his face and eyes possess a radiant luster—this is precisely why it is so.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "It is so!

Although a sovereign king may be peerless among humans for his excellence, if one were to place him beside a Cakravartin King, his facial features would appear extremely ugly and unattractive, resembling nothing more than a beggar standing beside a sovereign king."
The countenances of those emperors are still not as beautiful as the complexion of a Cakravartin king by a factor of hundreds of thousands of millions.

Just as a Cakravartin king is peerlessly and unsurpassedly handsome in the world, one who dwells beside the second-tier king would have a face so extremely ugly and unattractive that it would not even compare to the dignified and beautiful features of Śakra by a factor of hundreds of thousands of millions.

For example, those who dwell in the presence of Śakra, the Lord of Devas, have countenances that are exceedingly ugly and unattractive; they do not even equal the countenance of the Sixth Heavenly King, which is upright and beautiful, by hundreds of thousands of millions of times.

Suppose those who dwell among the bodhisattvas and arhats in the land of Amitābha Buddha were as ugly-faced as the Sixth Heavenly King; even so, their countenances would still not equal those of the bodhisattvas and arhats in Amitābha Buddha’s land, whose features are upright, handsome, and beautiful by a factor of hundreds of thousands of billions.
The Buddha said:
"The countenances of all the bodhisattvas and arhats in the land of Amitābha Buddha are entirely upright and peerlessly beautiful, second only to the Way of Nirvāṇa."

Within the lecture halls, monasteries, and residences where Amitābha Buddha, the bodhisattvas, and the arhats dwell, as well as upon the bathing pools both inside and outside, there are trees made of the seven treasures.

Within it are trees of pure gold, trees of pure silver, trees of pure crystal, trees of pure lapis lazuli, trees of pure white jade, trees of pure coral, and trees of pure amber; each kind stands in its own distinct row.
Among them, there are two kinds of precious substances combined to form single trees:
silver trees have silver roots and golden stems, silver branches and golden leaves, silver flowers and golden fruits;
golden trees have golden roots and silver stems, golden branches and silver leaves, golden flowers and silver fruits.
As for the crystal trees, they have crystal roots and lapis lazuli stems, crystal branches and lapis lazuli leaves, crystal flowers and lapis lazuli fruits;
as for the lapis lazuli trees, they have lapis lazuli roots and crystal stems, lapis lazuli branches and crystal leaves, lapis lazuli flowers and crystal fruits;
these two precious substances together form a single tree.
Furthermore, among them, there are four kinds of precious trees that grow together as single trees:
the crystal tree has a crystal root and a lapis lazuli trunk, with golden branches, silver leaves, crystal blossoms, and lapis lazuli fruit;
the lapis lazuli tree has a lapis lazuli root and a crystal trunk, with golden branches, silver leaves, crystal blossoms, and lapis lazuli fruit.
These four kinds of precious trees mutually support one another, each standing in its own distinct row.
Among them, there are also trees formed by five precious substances combined into one:
with silver roots, golden stems, crystal branches, lapis lazuli leaves, silver blossoms, and golden fruit.
As for the gold trees, they have golden roots and silver trunks, crystal branches and lapis lazuli leaves, coral flowers and silver fruits;
as for the crystal trees, they have crystal roots and lapis lazuli trunks, coral branches and silver leaves, gold flowers and lapis lazuli fruits;
as for the lapis lazuli trees, they have lapis lazuli roots and coral trunks, crystal branches and gold leaves, silver flowers and coral fruits.
As for the coral trees: they have coral roots and lapis lazuli trunks, crystal branches and golden leaves, silver blossoms and lapis lazuli fruits;
these five treasures together form a single tree, yet each part maintains its distinct character.
Among them, there are trees formed by six jewels combined into one:
the silver tree has a silver root and a golden trunk, crystal branches and lapis lazuli leaves, coral flowers and amber fruit.
As for the golden trees, they have roots of gold and stems of silver; branches of crystal and leaves of lapis lazuli; flowers of amber and fruits of coral.
As for the crystal trees, they have roots of crystal and stems of lapis lazuli; branches of coral and leaves of amber; flowers of silver and fruits of gold.
As for the lapis lazuli trees, they have roots of lapis lazuli and stems of coral; branches of amber and leaves of crystal; flowers of gold and fruits of silver.
These six kinds of precious trees mutually support one another, each standing in its own distinct row.
Among them, there are also some trees composed of seven treasures combined into a single trunk:
silver trees with silver roots and golden stems, crystal branches and lapis lazuli leaves, coral flowers and amber fruits.
As for the golden trees, they have roots of gold and stalks of crystal; branches of lapis lazuli, leaves of coral; flowers of amber and fruit of silver.
As for the crystal trees, they have roots of crystal and stalks of lapis lazuli; branches of coral, leaves of amber; flowers of musaragalva and fruit of white jade.
As for the coral trees, they have roots of coral and stalks of amber; branches of white jade, leaves of lapis lazuli; flowers of musaragalva and fruit of moon-pearls.
As for the amber trees, they have roots of amber and stems of white jade; branches of coral and leaves of lapis lazuli; with water-essence flowers and golden fruit.
As for the white jade trees, they have roots of white jade and stems of mother-of-pearl; branches of coral and leaves of amber; with golden blossoms and *maṇi* jewel fruit.

These trees made of the seven treasures mutually support one another; they are diverse and distinct in their various forms. Row meets row, stem aligns with stem, branch meets branch, leaf faces leaf, flower looks toward flower, and fruit corresponds with fruit.
The Buddha said:

"In the lecture hall and vihāra of Amitābha Buddha, there are inner and outer bathing pools made of the seven treasures, surrounded by rows of trees made of the seven treasures; likewise, among the bodhisattvas and arhats within their dwellings made of the seven treasures, there are inner and outer bathing pools surrounded by rows of trees made of the seven treasures, numbering in the hundreds and thousands, all arranged in such a manner."
Each produced the five musical tones, and their sounds were exceedingly beautiful and beyond compare.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

“The sounds of the hundred kinds of musical performances of a worldly monarch do not equal the excellence of the sounds of the various musical performances of a Cakravartin King, even by hundreds of thousands of millions of times.”

The sounds of the ten thousand kinds of musical instruments of a Cakravartin King are still not equal to even a single sound from the musical instruments of the gods in the second heaven, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, by a factor of hundreds of thousands of billions.

Even the sounds of the ten thousand kinds of musical performances in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven do not compare to the excellence of a single sound in the sixth heaven, being surpassed by it a hundred thousand billion times.

Even the sounds of the ten thousand kinds of celestial music in the sixth heaven do not equal the excellence of a single sound from a tree of the seven treasures in the land of Amitābha Buddha, by hundreds of thousands of billions of times.
In the land of Amitābha Buddha, there are also ten thousand kinds of natural musical performances, whose joy is infinitely great.
Whenever Amitābha Buddha, along with the various bodhisattvas and arhats, wishes to bathe, they may each enter their respective pools of the seven treasures to bathe.
If the bodhisattvas and arhats intend for the water to submerge their feet, the water immediately submerges their feet;
if they intend for the water to reach their knees, the water immediately reaches their knees;
if they intend for the water to reach their waists, the water immediately reaches their waists.
If he intended for the water to reach his armpits, the water immediately reached his armpits;
if he intended for the water to reach his neck, the water immediately reached his neck;
if he intended for the water to pour over his body from above, the water immediately poured over his body.
"If you wish for the water to return to its former state, it shall immediately return to its former state;
let it be as you desire, according to your pleasure.
The Buddha said:

"After Amitābha, along with all the bodhisattvas and arhats, have finished bathing, they each sit upon a great lotus flower; immediately, turbulent winds arise spontaneously from the four directions."
As for that turbulent wind, it is neither the wind of the world nor the wind of the heavens.
It is simply the essence of all the winds from the eight directions, above, and below, which naturally congeals and undergoes transformation.

It is neither cold nor hot, always harmoniously moderate and perfectly suited; it is exceedingly refreshing and incomparably excellent. It rises slowly, neither too tardy nor too swift, attaining the proper measure of suitability.
The seven-jeweled trees were stirred by the wind, producing the sounds of the five musical tones.
The blossoms of these seven-jeweled trees completely covered the land within the kingdom, scattering over the Buddha, the bodhisattvas, and the arhats.
The flowers fell to the ground, forming a layer four inches thick; they were exceedingly soft and exquisite, beyond compare.
Then, a natural wind arose and blew away the withered blossoms, clearing them all away spontaneously.

Immediately thereafter, natural winds arose from the four directions and blew upon the trees made of the seven treasures; the trees all produced the five musical tones, and their blossoms spontaneously scattered over the Buddha, the bodhisattvas, and the arhats.
The flowers, small and withered, fell to the ground and were immediately swept away by themselves.
Then, from the four directions, turbulent winds arose and blew upon the trees made of the seven treasures;
this occurred four times in succession.

Among the bodhisattvas and arhats, some desired only to hear the sutras; some desired only to hear music; some desired only to hear the fragrance of flowers. Some did not desire to hear the sutras; some did not desire to hear the sound of music;
some did not desire to hear the fragrance of flowers. Whatever they wished to hear, they immediately heard it alone;
those who did not wish to hear, heard nothing at all.
They enjoyed themselves according to their desires and were not thwarted in their wishes.

Having finished bathing, they each departed to practice the Way; among them were those who lectured on the sutras on the ground, those who recited the sutras, those who expounded the sutras, those who received the sutras orally, those who listened to the sutras, those who contemplated the sutras, those who reflected upon the Way, those who practiced seated meditation, and those who engaged in the practice of the sutras. Among them were also those who, in mid-air, lectured on the sutras, recited the sutras, expounded the sutras, received the sutras orally, listened to the sutras, contemplated the sutras, reflected upon the Way, practiced one-pointed seated meditation, and engaged in the practice of the sutras.
Those who had not yet attained the path of Srotāpanna immediately attained the path of Srotāpanna;
those who had not yet attained the path of Sakṛdāgāmin immediately attained the path of Sakṛdāgāmin;
those who had not yet attained the path of Anāgāmin immediately attained the path of Anāgāmin.
Those who had not yet attained the path of Arhatship immediately attained the path of Arhatship;
those who had not yet attained the stage of an Avaivartika Bodhisattva immediately attained the stage of an Avaivartika.
Each preached the sutras and practiced the Way, and all attained the Way, none of whom failed to rejoice and leap for joy.

"Among the bodhisattvas, there were those who desired to make offerings to the countless Buddhas of the eight directions, above, and below; they immediately all went forward together to pay homage to the Buddha, took their leave to depart, and set out to make offerings to the countless Buddhas of the eight directions, above, and below. The Buddha then granted his consent and permitted them to go."

All the bodhisattvas were filled with great joy; numbering in the hundreds of billions, incalculable and beyond measure, they were all endowed with wisdom and valor. Each leading their respective groups, they flew forth in pursuit of one another, dispersing together as they soared until they reached the presence of the innumerable Buddhas of the eight directions, above, and below.
They all stepped forward to pay homage to the Buddhas and immediately made offerings.

Desiring that ten thousand kinds of spontaneous objects appear before them, there instantly appeared a hundred kinds of flowers of various colors, a hundred kinds of variegated silks, a hundred kinds of karpāsa garments, lamps of the seven precious jewels, and ten thousand kinds of musical performances—all of which manifested before them.
These flowers and incenses are of ten thousand kinds; they are spontaneous phenomena, neither of this world nor of the heavens.
These ten thousand kinds of things are all produced through the transformative convergence of the various spontaneities throughout the eight directions, above, and below.
If they desire to obtain [something], it spontaneously manifests through transformation; if they do not wish for it, it vanishes by transformation.

The bodhisattvas then together uphold these [offerings] to make offerings to the Buddhas, the bodhisattvas, and the arhats, circumambulating them on all sides, in front, and behind; whatever they desire in their minds immediately arrives.
At that time, the joy was beyond words!

Each of the bodhisattvas desired a flower forty *li* in size, which immediately appeared naturally before them. They then held these together in mid-air and scattered them over the Buddhas, bodhisattvas, and arhats;

all remained suspended in the air, facing downward. The flowers were exceedingly fragrant and beautiful; when they slightly withered and fell to the ground, a natural whirlwind would blow, causing the withered flowers to vanish entirely.

The minds of the various bodhisattvas each desired eighty *li* worth of flowers; immediately, they appeared naturally before them, which they all took and scattered over the Buddhas, the bodhisattvas, and the arhats.
The flowers then turned downward in mid-air and, having slightly withered, fell to the ground. Thereupon, a natural turbulent wind blew, and the withered flowers were all spontaneously cleared away.

Each of the bodhisattvas further desired one hundred and sixty *li* of flowers; they immediately appeared naturally before them, and they together held them in mid-air and scattered them over the various Buddhas, bodhisattvas, and arhats.
The flowers then descended from mid-air toward the ground, slightly withered as they fell; immediately, a natural turbulent wind blew, and the withered flowers were all spontaneously cleared away.

The minds of the various bodhisattvas each desired further to obtain flowers three hundred and twenty li in size; these immediately appeared naturally before them. They then took them from the midst of the void and scattered them over the various Buddhas, bodhisattvas, and arhats.
As the flowers descended from the void toward the ground, they slightly withered and fell; immediately, a natural turbulent wind blew, and all the withered flowers were spontaneously cleared away.

Each of the bodhisattvas then desired to obtain flowers measuring six hundred and forty li; these immediately appeared naturally before them, and they scattered them over the various Buddhas, bodhisattvas, and arhats.
All remained suspended in mid-air facing downward, slightly withered as they fell to the ground, where a natural turbulent wind blew away the withered flowers.

Each of the bodhisattvas further desired to obtain flowers one thousand two hundred and eighty li in circumference; these immediately appeared naturally before them. They then held them together in mid-air and scattered them over the various Buddhas, bodhisattvas, and arhats.
While all were suspended in mid-air facing downward, they slightly withered and fell to the ground. A natural, turbulent wind then blew, and the withered flowers were all spontaneously carried away.

The minds of the various bodhisattvas each desired further to obtain flowers measuring two thousand five hundred and sixty li; these immediately appeared naturally before them. They then rose into the air together and scattered them over the various Buddhas, bodhisattvas, and arhats.
All remained suspended in mid-air facing downward, slightly withered as they fell to the ground. A turbulent wind blew away all the withered flowers, and they vanished naturally.

The minds of the various bodhisattvas each desired again to obtain five thousand one hundred and twenty *li* of flowers; these immediately appeared naturally before them. They then held them together in mid-air and scattered them over the various Buddhas, bodhisattvas, and arhats.
All remained suspended in mid-air facing downward, slightly withering as they fell to the ground. A turbulent wind blew away all the withered flowers, and they vanished naturally.

Each of the bodhisattvas then desired ten thousand two hundred and forty *li* worth of flowers; immediately, they all appeared naturally before them. They then held them together in mid-air and scattered them over the various Buddhas, bodhisattvas, and arhats.
As the flowers slightly withered and fell to the ground, a turbulent wind blew away all the withered blossoms, causing them to vanish naturally.

Each of the bodhisattvas further desired two hundred and forty-eight thousand *li* worth of flowers; these immediately appeared before them, and they together held them in the air and scattered them over the Buddhas, the bodhisattvas, and the arhats.

While still suspended in mid-air, the flowers turned downward and slightly withered as they fell to the ground; then, a turbulent wind blew away all the withered blossoms, and they vanished of their own accord.

Each of the bodhisattvas, wishing again to obtain flowers fifty *li* in circumference, found them all immediately before them; they then together held them aloft in mid-air and scattered them over the various Buddhas, bodhisattvas, and arhats.

As they remained suspended in the air facing downward, they slightly withered and fell to the ground, whereupon a turbulent wind blew away all the withered flowers, making them vanish of their own accord.

Each of the bodhisattvas further desired a hundred thousand *li* of flowers, which immediately appeared before them. The bodhisattvas then together took these flowers in the midst of the void and scattered them over the various Buddhas, bodhisattvas, and arhats.
While still suspended in the void, they turned downward; they withered slightly and fell to the ground, whereupon a turbulent wind blew away all the withered flowers, and they naturally vanished.

Each of the bodhisattvas further desired flowers spanning two hundred thousand *li*; these immediately appeared before them. They then held them together in mid-air and scattered them over the various Buddhas, bodhisattvas, and arhats.
As the flowers began to wither slightly and fall to the ground, a turbulent wind blew away all the withered blossoms, causing them to vanish naturally.

The minds of the various bodhisattvas each desired again to obtain flowers forty thousand *li* in circumference; these immediately appeared before them, and they together held them in the air and scattered them over the Buddhas, the bodhisattvas, and the arhats.
While all were in the air, they descended toward the ground and slightly withered as they fell; then, a turbulent wind blew away all the withered flowers, and they naturally vanished.

The minds of the various bodhisattvas each desired eighty thousand *li* of flowers; immediately, these appeared before them, and they together held them in the air and scattered them over the Buddhas, the bodhisattvas, and the arhats.
All remained suspended in mid-air, facing downward, until they slightly withered and fell to the ground; then, a turbulent wind blew away all the withered flowers, and they naturally vanished.

Each of the bodhisattvas thought of obtaining flowers one million six hundred thousand li in circumference; immediately, these appeared before them, which they all held and scattered over the various Buddhas, bodhisattvas, and arhats.
When the flowers slightly withered and fell to the ground, a turbulent wind blew away the withered blossoms, and they vanished of their own accord.

Each of the bodhisattvas thought of obtaining three million *li* worth of flowers; immediately, these appeared before them, which they all held and scattered over the various Buddhas, bodhisattvas, and arhats.
As the flowers slightly withered and fell to the ground, a turbulent wind blew away the withered blossoms of their own accord.

Each of the bodhisattvas thought of obtaining six million *li* worth of flowers; immediately, they all appeared before them, which they held together and scattered over the various Buddhas, bodhisattvas, and arhats.

The flowers spontaneously merged into a single flower, perfectly symmetrical and circular, with its circumference being exactly proportionate. This flower was twice as large as the previous ones, exceedingly soft and beautiful, surpassing the former flowers by several thousand times. Its colors were diverse and its fragrance was beyond description.

All the bodhisattvas were filled with great joy; together in the midst of the void, they produced a multitude of sounds through spontaneous music, delighting the Buddhas, the bodhisattvas, and the arhats.
At that time, the joy was beyond words.

All the bodhisattvas withdrew to sit and listen to the sutra; having finished listening, they all recited it from memory and mastered it, thereby gaining a deeper understanding of the Way of the sutras and further clarifying their wisdom.

Then, throughout the Buddha-lands, from the first heaven of the Four Great Kings up to the Heaven of the Thirty-three, all the devas together took various kinds of ten thousand natural celestial objects and descended to make offerings to the bodhisattvas and arhats.
The devas and humans all once again produced a great multitude of musical sounds and performances in the air.
Those devas and humans who had come forward moved aside to make way for those coming later;
those who came later likewise made offerings as before, while mutually yielding the space to one another.
The devas and humans listened to the sutra with joy, collectively performing great music; at that time, their happiness was boundless.

When the bodhisattvas had finished making offerings and listening to the sutra, they all rose, paid homage to the Buddha, and departed. They then immediately flew to the countless Buddhas of the eight directions, above, and below, where they made offerings and listened to the sutra, each acting exactly as before.

After they had finished traveling everywhere, before noon, each flew back to their own land, paid homage to Amitābha Buddha, and sat down to listen to the sutra; when it was finished, they were all greatly filled with joy.
The Buddha said:
"When Amitābha Buddha, along with the bodhisattvas and arhats, desire to eat, there spontaneously appear tables made of the seven precious substances, and seats made of layered karpāsika cloth."
Before the Buddha and all the bodhisattvas, there were naturally formed vessels of the seven precious gems, each containing food and drink of a hundred flavors.
This food and drink was unlike anything of the mundane world, nor was it of the heavens;

it was the most refined essence among the myriad natural foods of the eight directions, above, and below. It was incomparably fragrant and delicious, produced spontaneously by transformation. Whether one desired sweetness or acidity, one obtained whatever one wished for.

Among the various bodhisattvas and arhats, some desired gold bowls, some silver bowls, some crystal bowls, some coral bowls, some amber bowls, some white jade bowls, some musaragalva bowls, some agate bowls, some moon-pearl bowls, some maṇi-jewel bowls, and some purple-polished gold bowls; these arrived immediately according to their wishes.
Yet they came from nowhere, nor was there anyone who offered them; they were simply produced through spontaneous transformation.
All the bodhisattvas and arhats eat; their consumption is neither excessive nor deficient, being entirely equal.
They do not speak of food as good or bad, nor do they rejoice because it is delicious.
When the meal was finished, all the food, bowls, tables, and seats spontaneously vanished; they would only manifest again when it was time to eat.

Because the minds of the bodhisattvas and arhats were pure and clean, the food and drink served merely to provide physical strength; they all naturally dissolved away, being completely exhausted and transformed until nothing remained.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"When Amitābha Buddha preaches the sutra for the sake of the bodhisattvas and arhats, they all assemble together in the great lecture hall."

Countless bodhisattvas, arhats, and celestial beings and humans, beyond all calculation, all flew to the abode of Amitābha Buddha; they paid homage to the Buddha and withdrew to sit and listen to the sutra.

That Buddha extensively expounded the Great Sūtra of the Wisdom of the Path; all who heard it understood it fully, and there was none who did not rejoice with leaping hearts and attain liberation of mind.
Immediately, turbulent winds arose spontaneously from the four directions, blowing upon the trees of the seven treasures, which all produced the five musical tones.

Flowers from trees made of the seven treasures cover that land; they all hang downward in mid-air, and their fragrance pervades the entire country, scattering over Amitābha Buddha, as well as upon the bodhisattvas and arhats.
The flowers that fell to the ground were all four inches thick; as soon as they began to wither slightly, a turbulent wind blew them away, and the withered blossoms naturally departed.
In this manner, the turbulent winds from the four directions blew the flowers of the seven-jeweled trees four times over.

Then, from the first realm of the Four Heavenly Kings, up through the second realm of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and as far as the thirty-second heaven, all the devas and humans took with them ten thousand kinds of natural celestial objects—hundreds of varieties of multicolored flowers, hundreds of varieties of blended incenses, hundreds of varieties of mixed silks and brocades, and hundreds of varieties of karpāsa cotton garments—as well as ten thousand kinds of musical performances, each more exquisite and superior than the last. Carrying these, they descended one by one to pay homage to Amitābha Buddha, making offerings to the Buddha, the bodhisattvas, and the arhats.
All the devas and humans again performed great musical performances to delight Amitābha Buddha, as well as the bodhisattvas and arhats.
At that time, the joy was beyond words.
The various devas made way for one another, and those who arrived later offered worship just as those before them had done.
Thus, there were incalculable Buddha-lands in the eastern direction, their number beyond reckoning;
like the sands along the banks of the Ganges River, with one Buddha for every grain of sand, such was their number.

Each of the Buddhas dispatched countless, incalculable bodhisattvas, all of whom flew to the abode of Amitābha Buddha; they prostrated themselves and listened to the sutra, and being filled with great joy, they all rose, paid their respects once more, and departed as they had come.

In the western, northern, southern, and four intermediate directions, the Buddhas—each as numerous as the sands along the banks of the Ganges—each dispatched countless Bodhisattvas who flew to the abode of Amitābha Buddha; they prostrated and listened to the sutra in the same manner.

Then, from the regions below and above, Buddhas as numerous as the sands along the banks of the Ganges each dispatched bodhisattvas beyond all calculation; they flew to the abode of Amitābha Buddha, prostrated themselves, and listened to the sutra.
They will continue to open space for one another, and thus there will never be a time when this ceases.

The Buddha said, “The reason why all Buddhas take the sands flowing along the banks of the Ganges as their measure is that the Buddhas of the eight directions and the zenith and nadir are infinite in number; they are exceedingly vast and numerous, such that they can no longer be calculated individually. Therefore, the sands flowing along the banks of the Ganges are used as a measure.”
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
“When Amitābha Buddha has finished preaching the sutra for the bodhisattvas and arhats, those among the devas and humans who had not yet attained the Way will immediately attain it.”
Those who had not yet attained the stage of *srotāpanna* immediately attained the stage of *srotāpanna*;
those who had not yet attained the stage of *sakṛdāgāmin* immediately attained the stage of *sakṛdāgāmin*;
and those who had not yet attained the stage of *anāgāmin* immediately attained the stage of *anāgāmin*.
Those who have not yet attained arhatship shall immediately attain arhatship;
those who have not yet attained the stage of an avaivartika bodhisattva shall immediately attain the stage of an avaivartika bodhisattva.

Amitābha Buddha immediately accords with the aspirations and vows cherished by that person’s mind when seeking the Way in their past lives; according to their capacity, whether great or small, he preaches the sutras and bestows them upon them, causing them to quickly attain understanding and realization.
All were possessed of clear wisdom and each took delight in their own way; regarding the sūtras and the Way they sought, there was none who did not rejoice.
Those who recited and practiced them chanted and studied them until they were thoroughly mastered, never feeling weary or reaching an end.
Among the bodhisattvas and arhats, there were those who recited the sutras, their voices sounding like three hundred bells.

Among them were those who expounded the sutras, like the howling of a violent wind and torrential rain; thus they continued for the duration of an entire kalpa, never once succumbing to weariness or fatigue.
