They were all endowed with wisdom and valor, their bodies were light and agile, and they never experienced pain or itching.

Even when walking, sitting, or rising at the height of physical exertion, they were all skillful, robust, and courageous, like the king of lions in the deep mountains; wherever he turned his course, none dared to oppose him.
Free from any sense of doubt or difficulty, what he performs with his mind is beyond calculation by hundreds of thousands of millions of times.

Even the king of fierce lions is surpassed hundreds of thousands of millions of times; yet even that is not equal to my second disciple, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, who is hundreds of thousands of millions of times more courageous and valiant.
Just as Mahāmaudgalyāyana was peerless among the bodhisattvas and arhats in all lands—

surpassing them a hundred thousand ten-thousand million times in his flight and movement, his wisdom and valor, his clairvoyant vision and clairaudience, and his knowledge of matters of the eight directions, above and below, past, future, and present.
If these were combined into a single wisdom, it would still fall short by hundreds of thousands of billions of times compared to the wisdom of the arhats in the land of Amitābha Buddha.
The Bodhisattva Ajita immediately rose, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and asked the Buddha:
"In the land of Amitābha Buddha, are there any among the arhats who pass into parinirvāṇa?"
"I wish to hear it.
The Buddha said,
"If you wish to know, do you see the stars in these four continents?"
The Bodhisattva Ajita said,
"Indeed, I see it. The Buddha said:
"Just as my second disciple, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, flies up into the heavens for one day and night and counts to know exactly how many stars there are."
The stars in these four continents are exceedingly numerous and cannot be counted; yet there are still hundreds of thousands of billions of times more stars than these.
Suppose one were to remove a single drop from the great ocean of the world—could that cause the ocean water to decrease, or would one know it has become less?
He replied,
"Even if one were to subtract hundreds of thousands of billions of *dou* and *shi*, one still could not cause it to diminish enough to be perceived as less.
The Buddha said:

"In the land of Amitābha Buddha, although there may be among the arhats those who pass into parinirvāṇa, it is like the ocean being diminished by a single drop of water; it cannot cause the number of arhats remaining to be known as decreased or diminished."
The Buddha said,
“If one stream were removed from the great ocean, would it cause the ocean to diminish?
He replied:
"Even if one were to subtract hundreds of thousands of billions of mountain streams, it still could not be known that [the ocean] had diminished even slightly.
The Buddha said,
"If one were to subtract from the great ocean a single *gaṅgā* river's worth of water, would it be possible to know that it had diminished even slightly?"
He replied:
"Even if one were to subtract hundreds of thousands of billions of *gaṅgā* rivers' worth of water, it could not be reduced enough for it to be known as diminished.
The Buddha said:

"In the land of Amitābha Buddha, the number of arhats who have entered parinirvāṇa is immeasurable, and the number of those remaining who have newly attained the Way is likewise immeasurable; yet, there is no increase or decrease whatsoever."
The Buddha said:
"If all the waters in the world were to flow entirely into the great ocean, would it cause the water in the ocean to increase?
He replied:
"It cannot cause them to increase further.
Why is this? It is because this great ocean is the sovereign among all the waters and virtues of the world; therefore, it is able to do so."
The Buddha said:

"The land of Amitābha Buddha is also like this; it causes all the countless Buddhalands of the eight directions and the zenith and nadir, including the innumerable devas, humans, and even the crawling and flying insects, to be reborn there in such vast numbers that they can no longer be calculated."

In the land of Amitābha Buddha, the various bodhisattvas, arhats, and the assembly of bhikṣus remain as they were before; there is not even a single dharma that differs, and this constitutes their increase.
Why is this so? Because the land of Amitābha Buddha is the most excellent.

Among the countless Buddha-lands of the eight directions and above and below, it is the sovereign of all that is good, the hero among Buddha-lands, the jewel among Buddha-lands, where the lifespan is the longest and most enduring, the most eminent among Buddha-lands, the most vast among Buddha-lands, and the capital among Buddha-lands. It is spontaneously unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskṛta*), most excellent, brilliant, beautiful, and possesses infinite, supreme bliss.

Why is this so? It is because when Amitābha Buddha was originally a bodhisattva, his vows were courageous and fierce, and he practiced with diligence and without indolence; it is through the accumulation of such merit that he has been able to achieve this.
The Bodhisattva Ajita was immediately filled with great joy; kneeling on his right knee with palms joined, he said:
"The Buddha has described the land of Amitābha Buddha as swift, virtuous, bright, excellent, and most exquisite beyond compare—is it truly so alone?"
The Buddha said:
"In the land of Amitābha Buddha, within the dwellings made of the seven treasures where the bodhisattvas and arhats reside, some are situated in mid-air and some are upon the ground;
among them, if any should wish for their dwelling to be the highest, that dwelling immediately becomes high."
Among them, those who wished for their dwellings to be the largest had their dwellings become large;
those who wished for their dwellings to be in the midst of space had their dwellings appear in space;
all were spontaneously able to act according to their will.
Among them, there are those who are utterly unable to cause their dwellings to conform to their wishes. Why is this so?

Those who are able to cause their dwellings to conform to their wishes are all ones who, in previous lives while seeking the Way, practiced with a compassionate mind and diligence, performed many good deeds, and attained such results through the weight of their merit.

Among them, those who are particularly incapable are all such because in their past lives, when seeking the Way, they did not practice diligence with a compassionate heart nor increase their performance of various good deeds; this is the result of their meager virtue.
Regarding their clothing and food, these are all spontaneously provided and equal.
Although there are differences in the magnitude of their virtues, he distinguishes their heroic prowess so that the multitude may behold it.
The Buddha asked,
"Do you see the dwelling place of the sixth Heavenly King?
[He replied,] "Indeed, I see it."
The Buddha said:
"The lecture halls and residences in the land of Amitābha Buddha are all hundreds of thousands of billions of times superior to the abode of the Sixth Heavenly King."

All bodhisattvas and arhats possess the power of clear vision and penetrating hearing, perceiving and knowing all matters of the eight directions, above and below, as well as those of the past, future, and present.

Furthermore, he knows the thoughts—whether good or evil—in the minds of countless beings in the heavens above and the world below, as well as all species of crawling and creeping creatures; he knows all that they intend to say with their mouths.

He knows in what year and in what kalpa they shall attain liberation, attain the human path, or be reborn in the land of Amitābha Buddha; he knows that they shall become bodhisattvas or arhats, knowing all this in advance.
Upon the crowns of all bodhisattvas and arhats there is naturally their own radiance, which illuminates to varying degrees—some great, some small.
Among the bodhisattvas, there are two most honored ones who always sit in attendance to the left and right of the Buddha to attend to his formal discourses;
the Buddha constantly sits facing these two bodhisattvas together, deliberating upon matters of the eight directions, above and below, and of the past, future, and present.
If one wishes to cause these two bodhisattvas to travel to the countless Buddhas of the eight directions, above, and below, they shall immediately fly there;
they can travel by flight wherever their hearts desire, as swiftly as a Buddha, with incomparable valor and vigor.
One of those bodhisattvas was named Gailou-xiong (Kāśyapa), and the other was named Mohena-po (Mahānāman).

Their radiance and wisdom were foremost; from the crests of their heads, light shone forth in blazing flames, constantly illuminating the Buddha-lands of a thousand Mount Sumerus in other directions with perpetual brilliance.
The light from the crowns of the heads of those bodhisattvas each illuminates a thousand billion *li*, while the light from the crowns of the heads of the arhats each illuminates seven *zhang*.
The Buddha said:

"If people of the world—whether good men or good women—who face urgent fear or matters involving government officials, simply take refuge in these Bodhisattvas, Gaṇeśvara and Mahānābha, there shall be none who do not attain liberation."
The Buddha told Bodhisattva Ajita:
"The light from the crown of Amitābha Buddha’s head is an immense radiance.

The sun, moon, and stars, all dwelling and abiding in the void of space, can no longer revolve or move in their courses; they also lack any brilliant luster, for their brightness is entirely eclipsed and is no longer seen."
The Buddha’s radiance illuminates his land, and its flames shine upon the buddha-lands of other directions, remaining perpetually and brilliantly bright, never reaching a time of darkness.

In that land, there is no such thing as one day or two days, nor five days or ten days; there are no fifteen days or one month, nor five months or ten months; there are no five years or ten years, nor a hundred years or a thousand years, nor ten thousand years or a hundred million years, nor a hundred, a thousand, ten thousand, or a hundred million years.

There is no single kalpa, ten kalpas, a hundred kalpas, or a thousand kalpas; there are no ten thousand kalpas or a million kalpas, nor ten million kalpas, a hundred million kalpas, or a billion kalpas.
The radiance of Amitābha Buddha is infinitely bright; even after countless kalpas, further countless kalpas, and again countless, incalculable kalpas, it shall never come to a time of darkness.
The land and its various devas shall never suffer destruction or decay.
Why is this? Because the lifespan of Amitābha Buddha is exceedingly long and his land is most excellent; therefore, it is able to be so!
The lifespan of that Buddha shall endure for incalculable kalpas, and even after further incalculable kalpas, he will not yet enter parinirvāṇa.

He shall continue to teach within the world, intending to deliver the countless buddha-fields of the eight directions, above and below, including all devas, humans, and even the smallest crawling insects. He desires that they all be reborn in his land and that they all attain the path of nirvāṇa.
Those who become bodhisattvas all desire to cause everyone else to become buddhas.

Once they have become buddhas, they in turn teach and transform the devas, humans, and all creatures—whether flying, crawling, or wriggling—in the eight directions, above, and below, desiring that they too shall become buddhas.
Having become a Buddha, he further instructs the countless devas, humans, and all classes of wriggling and creeping creatures, causing them all to attain the path of Nirvana.

Those disciples who are capable of being taught shall, in turn, teach one another and successively deliver one another, leading them until they attain the stages of *srotāpanna*, *sakṛdāgāmin*, *anāgāmin*, *arhat*, or the path of a *pratyekabuddha*. Thus, through successive mutual deliverance, all shall likewise attain the path of *nirvāṇa*.
They have not yet entered parinirvāṇa; those delivered and liberated by Amitābha Buddha continue in this manner from one to another.
They remain for incalculable kalpas, for countless upon countless kalpas, beyond all calculation, and there will never be a time when they enter parinirvāṇa.

The countless devas and human beings of the eight directions, above and below, as well as all classes of wriggling and crawling creatures who are born in the land of Amitābha Buddha and shall become Buddhas, are beyond further calculation.
Those who have become arhats and attained the path to nirvāṇa are likewise incalculable, beyond all measure.

The grace and virtue of Amitābha Buddha, and all that he bestows throughout the eight directions and the zenith and nadir, are infinite and boundless; they are profoundly deep, immeasurable, and their sublime goodness is beyond words.

The sūtras and paths that emerge from his wisdom and instruction are proclaimed throughout the eight directions, above and below, across the countless heavens and the world of men; they are truly unfathomable.
"The number of these sutra scrolls is exceedingly vast, beyond further calculation, and has no limit whatsoever.
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Ajita:
"Do you wish to know whether the lifespan of Amitābha Buddha is infinite or not?"
They replied,
"We all wish to hear and know it.
The Buddha said:
"Listen clearly!

Throughout the countless Buddha-lands of the eight directions, above, and below, may all the devas, humans, and even the smallest crawling insects be enabled to enter the Way; may they all become Pratyekabuddhas and Arhats, sitting together in single-minded dhyāna, uniting their wisdom into one courageous power, desiring together to calculate and know the lifespan of Amitābha Buddha—how many thousands of billions of kalpas and years it is—but none at all are able to calculate or know it."

Furthermore, in each of the other directions, within Buddha-lands containing a thousand Mount Sumerus, all the devas, humans, and even the smallest crawling insects were enabled to enter the Way; they were all made into Pratyekabuddhas and Arhats, and were all made to sit in meditation with single-minded focus. When their wisdom was combined into a single courageous power to count the number of Bodhisattvas and Arhats in the land of Amitābha Buddha—how many thousands of billions of people there were—not a single person was able to know that number.
The lifespan of Amitābha is exceedingly long; vast and expansive, it is brilliantly illuminated. His wisdom is profoundly deep, boundless and bottomless—who could possibly know it or believe in it?
"Only the Buddha himself knows this with such confidence!
When Bodhisattva Ajita heard these words of the Buddha, he was greatly rejoiced; kneeling with palms joined, he said:

"The Buddha has spoken of Amitābha Buddha’s exceedingly long life span, his majestic and honored divinity, and his wisdom and radiance, which are so lofty, sublime, and excellent—truly, it is only thus."
The Buddha said:
“When Amitābha Buddha finally enters parinirvāṇa, the Bodhisattva Ghalo-xun (Kāśyapa) shall then become a Buddha.”

He presides over the wisdom of the Path and governs the instruction of all beings—gods and humans throughout the world and the eight directions, above and below, as well as all classes of crawling and flying creatures—causing them all to attain the Buddha’s way of Nirvana.

His wholesome merit shall likewise be like that of the Great Master Amitābha Buddha; he shall abide for incalculable kalpas, incalculable kalpas, beyond further reckoning, conforming to the Dharma as a Great Master, before finally entering parinirvāṇa.
Next, the Bodhisattva Mahānābha shall also become a Buddha.
He will preside over wisdom and lead the instruction of others; the merit of those he delivers across shall likewise be equal to that of the Great Master Amitābha Buddha.
They shall abide for incalculable kalpas and yet still not enter parinirvāṇa;
they shall successively transmit and uphold one another, so that the Way of the Sūtras is exceedingly clear and the lands are most excellent.
"Such is this Dharma; it shall never be interrupted, nor can it be exhausted.
Ānanda knelt with his hands joined in reverence and asked the Buddha:
"In the land of Amitābha Buddha, there is no Mount Sumeru; upon what, then, do the first four heavens and the second Trāyastriṃśa Heaven rely for their support and abiding?"
"I wish to hear it.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Do you have any doubts regarding the Buddha?"

Throughout the eight directions, above and below, infinite and boundless, limitless and immeasurable—the waters of all the heavens and the great oceans—if a single person were to measure them with a peck-measure, they might still be exhausted until their bottom mud is reached;
but the Buddha’s wisdom is not like this.
The Buddha said:

"As for those past Buddhas whom I have seen and known—those whose name was Śākyamuni Buddha, just as mine—I see them to be as numerous as the grains of sand along the banks of the Ganges River, with one Buddha for every single grain of sand."
All future Buddhas whose names shall be like mine will be as numerous as the grains of sand along the banks of the Ganges River.
Those who have only just begun to seek to become Buddhas, whose names shall be like mine, will also be as numerous as the grains of sand along the banks of the Ganges River.
The Buddha sat upright facing directly south, gazing toward the southern direction.
The Buddhas currently existing there whose names are the same as mine are as numerous as the grains of sand along the banks of the Ganges River.

In the eight directions, above and below, all the Buddhas of the past, future, and present who bear the same name as mine— each as numerous as the sands along the banks of ten Ganges Rivers, with one Buddha for every grain of sand, their number being thus great—
all these Buddhas have already foreseen and known this.
The Buddha said:

"In the past, throughout incalculable kalpas—whether one kalpa, ten kalpas, a hundred kalpas, a thousand kalpas, ten thousand kalpas, a hundred million kalpas, or hundreds of billions of kalpas—there have been Buddhas."

All the Buddhas who have already passed away—whether one Buddha, ten Buddhas, a hundred Buddhas, a thousand Buddhas, ten thousand Buddhas, a hundred million Buddhas, or hundreds of billions of Buddhas—each had a different name; none possessed a name identical to mine.

Just as the future kalpas begin—whether one kalpa, ten kalpas, a hundred kalpas, a thousand kalpas, ten thousand kalpas, a hundred million kalpas, or hundreds of billions of kalpas—there shall be Buddhas within those kalpas.

There is one Buddha, ten Buddhas, a hundred Buddhas, a thousand Buddhas, ten thousand Buddhas, a hundred million Buddhas, and a hundred trillion Buddhas; each has a distinct name, and only from time to time does there appear a single Buddha whose name is the same as mine.

In the countless Buddha-lands of the eight directions, above, and below, there are Buddhas currently residing; furthermore, in other lands beyond these—whether in one Buddha-land, ten Buddha-lands, a hundred Buddha-lands, a thousand Buddha-lands, ten thousand Buddha-lands, a hundred million Buddha-lands, or a hundred trillion Buddha-lands—there are Buddhas, each having their own names, which are numerous and diverse, and none of them bear the same name as mine.
Among the countless Buddhas of the eight directions, above, and below, one such as I appears only from time to time!

Throughout the eight directions, above, and below—past, future, and present—the interval between them is vast and remote, stretching out infinitely and boundlessly. Yet the Buddha’s wisdom is pervasive and exceedingly clear; it probes the past and knows the present, foreknowing the infinite without end and beholding the yet-to-be-occur without limit. This foresight is so boundless that it can never again be calculated.
The majestic spiritual power and sublime brilliance of innumerable Buddhas are all fully known by him.

The Buddha’s wisdom and the light of his moral virtue are so perfectly integrated that there is no one at all capable of questioning him regarding the ultimate depths of the Buddhist scriptures and the Way; the Buddha’s wisdom can never be measured or exhausted.
Upon hearing the Buddha’s words, Ānanda was seized with great terror and his hair stood on end;
he addressed the Buddha, saying, “I do not dare harbor any doubt regarding the Buddha.”

The reason I ask the Buddha is that in the Buddha-lands of other directions, there are all Mount Sumerus, upon which the First Heaven of the Four Great Kings and the Second Trāyastriṃśa Heaven all rely for their dwelling.
I fear that after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, there may be devas, humans, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās who come to ask me:
"In the land of Amitābha Buddha, why is it that Mount Sumeru alone does not exist?"
"As for the first, the Four Heavenly Kings, and the second, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven—by what causes and conditions do they abide?
I ought to answer them.
If I do not ask the Buddha now, after the Buddha has departed, with what words shall I respond when they question me?"
"Only the Buddha knows this himself; no one else is able to explain it for me.
For this reason, I ask the Buddha!
The Buddha said:
“Ānanda! From these third Yāma Heaven and fourth Tuṣita Heaven, up to the seventh Brahmā Heaven, upon what do they all depend and by what cause do they abide?”
Ānanda said:
"These devas all dwell naturally in the midst of space; they abide and reside in space, without any support or cause."
“The Buddha’s majestic power is exceedingly profound; he acts spontaneously according to his will. Whatever he intends to do, he does it without prior deliberation.
All these devas remain stationed in the midst of the void.”
"How much more so, then, regarding the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, which is so venerable that he desires to perform any deed?
Hearing these words of the Buddha, Ānanda was immediately filled with great joy; kneeling with palms joined, he said:

"The Buddha’s wisdom knows the affairs of the eight directions, above and below, of the past, future, and present—boundless, infinite, and without limit. It is exceedingly lofty, vast, wondrous, supreme, and excellent; it is utterly brilliant, peerless, and incomparable. His majestic spiritual power is so venerable that it cannot be resisted."

The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Ajita: "Among the people of this world, if there are good men or good women who wish to be reborn in the land of Amitābha Buddha, there are three classes;
because the virtues they have cultivated vary in magnitude, they do not reach one another."
The Buddha said:
"What are the three grades?

The first and most superior grade consists of those who leave home, abandon their wives and children, sever their desires, and practice as śramaṇas; they proceed toward the path of the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) and practice the bodhisattva path by upholding the sūtras of the six pāramitās."

Having become a śramaṇa, one does not violate the sūtras or the precepts; with a compassionate mind and diligent effort, one should not give way to anger, nor should one engage in sexual intercourse with women.

Maintaining the purity of the fast and precepts, with a mind free from greed or longing, one sincerely vows to be reborn in the land of Amitābha Buddha; thus, one constantly maintains this mindfulness with a sincere heart without interruption.
When that person seeks the Way in this present life, they will naturally see Amitābha Buddha, as well as various bodhisattvas and arhats, within their dreams while resting in bed.

When that person’s life is about to end, Amitābha Buddha will personally fly there with various bodhisattvas and arhats to welcome them; they shall then be reborn in the land of Amitābha Buddha, spontaneously manifesting by transformation within lotus flowers in ponds of the seven treasures.
He immediately attained a natural body of great stature and became an *avaivartika* bodhisattva.
Thereupon, he flew together with the other bodhisattvas to make offerings to the countless Buddhas of the eight directions, above, and below.
They immediately attain wisdom and valor, delighting in listening to the Way of the sutras, their hearts filled with joy.
Their dwellings, made of the seven treasures, abide in the midst of space, following their every wish at will.
"Whatever one desires to accomplish, one will draw near to Amitābha Buddha.
The Buddha said:

"All who wish to be reborn in the land of Amitābha Buddha should diligently uphold the sutras and precepts and practice such supreme dharmas as these; then they shall attain rebirth in the land of Amitābha Buddha and become worthy of the respect of the multitude."
"These are the foremost and highest class.
The Buddha said:

"As for those of the middle class, these are people who wish to be reborn in the land of Amitābha Buddha, yet are unable to leave their homes, abandon their wives and children, and sever their desires to become śramaṇas."

One should uphold the sutras and precepts without allowing them to decline or be lost; one should increase the practice of giving through almsgiving (dāna), always believing in and receiving the profound words of the Buddha’s sutras, and act with utmost sincerity and faith.
One should provide food for the śramaṇas, construct Buddhist temples and erect stupas, scatter flowers, burn incense, light lamps, and hang various silk banners and streamers.
Regarding such dharmas, one should maintain no sense of partiality or bias.
One should not give way to anger, but maintain the purity of the precepts and fasts; with a compassionate mind and diligent effort, one must sever thoughts of craving and desire.
If one desires to be reborn in the land of Amitābha Buddha, one should not cease these practices for even a single day or night.
That person shall see Amitābha Buddha even in this present life, and likewise within their dreams while lying down to rest.
When that person’s life is about to end, Amitābha Buddha will immediately manifest a transformation body, causing that person’s own eyes to behold Amitābha Buddha and his land.
"Those who go to the land of Amitābha Buddha shall attain wisdom and valor.
The Buddha said:

"If a person practices such acts of giving, yet later feels regret and harbors doubts in their heart—disbelieving that the performance of various good deeds through almsgiving will yield blessings in future lives, disbelieving in the existence of Amitābha Buddha’s land, and disbelieving in rebirth in that land—"
Even so, if that person continues their mindfulness without interruption— though perhaps believing for a moment and disbelieving for a moment, with a hesitant mind lacking firm resolve—
they shall attain rebirth there by virtue of maintaining their original virtuous aspiration as the foundation.
When that person’s life is nearing its end and they are on the verge of death, Amitābha Buddha will immediately manifest a transformed image so that the person may see it with their own eyes.
Though they can no longer speak, their heart will be filled with joy and exultation as they think to themselves:
"I regret not having known to increase my observance of the precepts and perform good deeds; now I shall be reborn in the land of Amitābha Buddha."
That person immediately felt remorse in their heart; because they repented, their illness slightly abated, though there was nothing more that could be done.
When that person’s life came to an end, they were reborn in the land of Amitābha Buddha.

Unable to proceed further to the presence of Amitābha Buddha, they suddenly see on the way, at the edge of Amitābha Buddha’s land, a city of natural seven-jeweled gems; their hearts are filled with great joy, and they stop within that city.
He was then born by transformation within a lotus flower in a pond of the seven treasures; his body grew naturally to full size.
He resided within that city for five hundred years, the city being two thousand li in both width and length.
Within the city there were also dwellings made of the seven treasures, both inside and out, containing bathing pools made of the seven treasures.
These bathing pools were naturally surrounded by flowers and incense, and above the pools stood rows upon rows of trees made of the seven treasures;
these likewise produced the sounds of the five musical notes.
When they wish to eat, there spontaneously appears before them food of a hundred flavors;
whatever they desire to obtain arrives according to their wishes.
Those people are also joyful within the city, and the city is like the natural objects of the second heaven, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.

Nevertheless, although that person cannot escape from within the city nor obtain a vision of Amitābha Buddha, they merely perceive his radiance; their hearts feel self-reproach, and they experience leaping joy.
Furthermore, they will be unable to hear the sutras;
furthermore, they will be unable to see the community of bhikṣus;
and furthermore, they will be unable to see or know what the appearances and characteristics of the bodhisattvas and arhats in the land of Amitābha Buddha are like.
Such sorrows and sufferings as those were to that person merely like a minor pleasure.
The Buddha did not cause his body to act; rather, he attained what was to be done spontaneously, as his mind naturally inclined toward the Way, and entered the city.

When that person originally sought the Way in past lives, their mind and speech were at variance; their words and thoughts lacked sincerity, and they harbored doubts regarding the Buddhist scriptures.
Furthermore, because they did not place faith in them, they would naturally have entered the evil realms;
yet Amitābha Buddha, out of compassion, used his majestic spiritual power to lead them away from there.
That person shall remain within the city for five hundred years before finally being able to depart.
Upon going to the presence of Amitābha Buddha to hear the sutra, their mind will not attain understanding;
furthermore, they shall not be permitted to listen to the sutra among the assembly of bodhisattvas, arhats, and bhikṣus.
Because they have left their dwelling places and houses on the earth, they cannot cause those houses to rise at will into the void to become tall and lofty.
Furthermore, they are very far away from Amitābha Buddha and are unable to draw near to him.
That person’s wisdom is not clear and their knowledge of the sutras is meager; their mind does not rejoice and their intellect is not yet resolved.

After a long time, that person will naturally attain clarity of wisdom and understanding of the sutras, becoming bright, vigorous, and courageous; their mind shall rejoice, and subsequently they shall become like the first class mentioned above.

Why is this so? It is because when that person was seeking the Way in their past lives, they did not strictly observe the precepts of fasting, they defiled and lost the sutras and Dharma, and their will was filled with doubt. They did not believe the Buddha’s words, nor did they believe in the profundity of the Buddhist scriptures. They did not believe that by practicing *dāna* and giving alms, one would obtain merit and blessings in future lives;
furthermore, they harbored regrets midway and did not believe in rebirth in the land of Amitābha Buddha. Because their cultivation of virtue lacked sincerity, such is the result.
"This is the second intermediate grade.
The Buddha said:

"As for those of the third grade, these are people who wish to be reborn in the land of Amitābha Buddha, yet they have no means to practice *dāna* (charitable giving), nor can they burn incense, scatter flowers, light lamps, hang various silk banners, build Buddhist temples or erect stupas, or provide food for the śramaṇas."

One should sever craving and desire, having no longing or attachment; one should attain swift compassion and diligent effort, refrain from anger, and maintain the purity of the precepts—such is the Dharma.
If one single-mindedly contemplates rebirth in the land of Amitābha Buddha and does not cease for ten days and nights, at the end of one's life,
one will immediately be reborn in the land of Amitābha Buddha, where one shall receive honor and possess courageous wisdom.
The Buddha said: "If,

after having performed such deeds, that person subsequently regrets them and their mind becomes wavering and doubtful— disbelieving that by performing good they shall obtain blessings in future lives,
and disbelieving in rebirth in the land of Amitābha Buddha— "
Although such a person may be thus, they will nonetheless attain rebirth.
When that person’s life is nearing its end and their illness is about to conclude, Amitābha Buddha will cause them to see the land of Amitābha Buddha within their dreams while lying in bed.
With great joy in his heart, he thought to himself:
"I regret that I did not recognize the benefit of performing various good deeds; now I shall be reborn in the land of Amitābha Buddha."

That person merely thought this, unable to speak further; he immediately repented his transgression, and by repenting, his offense was diminished and reduced, so that there was nothing more to be done.
When that person’s life comes to an end, they will immediately be reborn in the land of Amitābha Buddha.

If they are unable to reach it directly, they will instead see, along the way, a city of seven treasures extending two thousand li; their heart will be filled with singular joy, and they will take up residence therein.
Furthermore, they are born by transformation within lotuses in bathing pools made of the seven treasures, where their bodies spontaneously grow to maturity.
Their city is also like the aforementioned cities, resembling the spontaneous objects found in the second heaven, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
That person likewise remains within the city for another five hundred years before finally being able to emerge.
Upon reaching the presence of Amitābha Buddha, his heart is filled with great joy.
However, when that person hears the sutras, his mind does not attain understanding, his spirit finds no delight, his wisdom is not clarified, and he knows little of the scriptures.
Their dwelling places remain fixed upon the earth, unable to be raised at will into the void;
furthermore, they are very far from Amitābha Buddha and cannot draw near to him—this is likewise the case for those of the second grade, the middling class, who harbor doubts.

After a long time, that person shall also attain the opening and understanding of wisdom; becoming courageous in their knowledge of the sutras, their mind shall be filled with joy, and they will rank as the first class mentioned above.

Why is this so? It is because in their previous lives, while seeking the Way, they harbored regrets and doubts; they believed for a moment and then did not believe for a moment. They did not believe that performing good deeds would yield their blessings and virtues, yet they nonetheless naturally obtained them all.

According to their respective merits, some possess the capacity for elevation while others do not; each naturally proceeds toward their own course, preaching the sutras and practicing the Way with such distinction that they surpass one another by millions, remaining utterly beyond reach of comparison.
The Buddha said:
"Those who wish to seek the path of a bodhisattva and be born in the land of Amitābha Buddha shall, thereafter, all attain the stage of an avaivartika bodhisattva."

Those who are bodhisattvas of non-retrogression shall all possess the thirty-two marks and the golden hue of refined purple, as well as the eighty secondary characteristics; they shall all become buddhas.
In accordance with their vows, wherever they may seek to become Buddhas in other Buddha-lands, they shall never again fall into the realms of hell-beings, animals, or hungry ghosts (preta).
According to their diligent pursuit of the Way, whether it be morning or evening, the results are equal and identical.
"If one seeks the Way without ceasing, one will surely attain it; one shall not fail to obtain what one desires and aspires for.
The Buddha told Ajita and the other bodhisattvas:

"O devas, emperors, and people, I tell you all: those who wish to be reborn in the land of Amitābha Buddha, even if they cannot practice great diligence, meditative concentration, or uphold the sutras and precepts, must at the very least perform good deeds."
First, one must not kill living beings.
Second, one must not steal.
Third, one must not engage in lewdness or illicit passion with the wives of others.
Fourth, one must not be frivolous or deceitful.
Fifth, one must not drink alcohol.
Sixth, one must not engage in double-tongued speech.
Seventh, one must not engage in harsh speech.
Eighth, one must not engage in false speech.
Ninth, one must not harbor jealousy.
Tenth, one must not be greedy for food, nor harbor stinginess in the heart; one must not give way to anger, nor succumb to delusion, nor follow the cravings of the mind.
One must not harbor regret in one's heart, nor entertain doubt. One should practice filial piety and obedience;

one should practice utmost sincerity, loyalty, and trustworthiness. One should believe and accept that the words of the Buddha’s sutras are profound, and one should believe that by performing good deeds, one will obtain their blessings in future lives.

Those who uphold this teaching without allowing it to decline or be lost will attain rebirth in the land of Amitābha Buddha according to their aspirations, provided they observe the precepts with single-minded purity and constantly contemplate rebirth in the land of Amitābha Buddha day and night for ten days and ten nights without interruption. I shall compassionately regard them all and cause them to be born in the land of Amitābha Buddha.
The Buddha said:

“There are those in the world who, out of aspiration and wisdom, dwell at home while practicing goodness as a path; though they live with their wives and children amidst affectionate desires, amidst many anxieties and heavy domestic burdens that leave no leisure for great fasts or single-minded purity, even if they cannot leave home and renounce desire, when they have moments of leisure, they should rectify their own minds, contemplate the body, perform good deeds, and single-mindedly practice the Way for ten days and ten nights.”

If one is truly unable to do so, yet reflects deeply and deliberates with the desire to liberate oneself, one should at the very least sever all thoughts and cast off anxiety; do not dwell on household affairs, and do not share a bed with women.

By rectifying one's own body and mind and severing all craving and desire, maintaining the purity of the *upavāsa* precepts with single-minded devotion, and directing one’s thoughts toward rebirth in the Land of Amitābha Buddha without interruption for even one day and one night, all such persons shall, at the end of their lives, be reborn in that land. There they will be born by transformation within lotus flowers in bathing pools made of the seven treasures; they will attain wisdom and valor, and the seven-jeweled mansions in which they dwell will manifest according to their every wish.
"They shall be ranked next to the first class mentioned above.
The Buddha spoke to the Bodhisattva Ajita:
"The countless devas, humans, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās from the eight directions and the zenith and nadir who are reborn in the land of Amitābha Buddha—"
The great assembly gathered together at the bathing pool of the seven treasures.

Every single person sat upon a large lotus flower, each recounting their own cultivation of the Way and practice of goodness. Everyone spoke individually of their past lives and destinies when they sought the Way, the precepts they observed, the wholesome dharmas they performed, the origins and details of their births, the sūtras and the Way they delighted in, their wisdom in understanding the sūtras, and the merits of the deeds they had carried out; these accounts proceeded from the highest to the lowest, circulating through the entire assembly.

By knowing that the sutras have both clarity and obscurity, that wisdom has depth and shallowness, greatness and smallness, and that virtue has superiority and inferiority, abundance and scarcity, one distinguishes and knows the Way of Nature.
Their talents and wisdom are robust and fierce; they observe all phenomena with discernment, and their propriety and harmony cause them all to rejoice and leap for joy.
Their wisdom possesses valor and vigor, yet each remains distinct and independent of the others.
The Buddha said:
"That person did not cultivate merit beforehand; they treated doing good with frivolity and playfulness, and it was due to a lack of faith that this came to pass.
They were idle and negligent, acting as they pleased."
When the time came for the assembly to gather and discourse on the Way of the Sutras, [the others] were naturally pressed by haste, and their responses were slow and delayed.
His wisdom regarding the Way was exceptionally eminent and transcendent, his talent lofty and formidable; he alone remained weak at the periphery.
"To regret only when faced with the matter is of no further benefit once the regret has already emerged;
it merely results in a heart full of distress and longing for what one could have attained.
The Buddha said:
"The assembly of bodhisattvas and arhats in the land of Amitābha Buddha gather spontaneously in a great congregation.
Restraining their minds and governing their intentions, they maintain upright bodies and correct conduct, sporting with profound mastery."
They fly together in succession, alternating their entry and exit, making offerings without limit.
With hearts full of joy and delight, they observe the path of practice together, harmonizing and cultivating for a long time.
Possessing courageous wisdom and a resolve as vast as space, he strives with diligence toward his vows.
His mind never again wavers, his intent never again turns back, and there is never a time when he succumbs to weariness.
Although one seeks the Way, appearing outwardly slow and leisurely while remaining inwardly swift and urgent, one dwells in a state of spacious emptiness, attaining the perfect mean.
When the inner and outer correspond, there is spontaneous dignity and order.
Restrained and upright, with body and mind pure, they are free from craving and desire; they harbor no greed for anything and possess no evil flaws or impurities.
Their aspirations are each stable and excellent, without increase or decrease.
Seeking the Way with harmony and rectitude, one must not err or lean toward depravity.
Measuring oneself against the Dharma and following the constraints of the sutras, one dares not deviate or stumble.

Whether in the eight directions, above, or below—without boundaries or limits, acting with sovereign freedom as desired, reaching the infinite and the boundless—one does so entirely for the sake of the Way.
Vast and expansive, as well as open and boundless, one contemplates the Way with a mind free from other thoughts.
Without anxiety or concern, one is naturally non-active; established in emptiness and voidness, one is magnanimously at peace and free from desire.
Having formed virtuous vows, he sought with all his heart; harboring compassion and pity, he was diligent both inwardly and outwardly, such that his conduct accorded perfectly with ritual propriety.
Penetrating and unobstructed, harmonious and compliant, his inner and outer states were consistent;
having transcended to liberation, he was able to ascend into Nirvana, forever united in clarity with the Way and its Virtue.
Naturally maintaining its own characteristics, the nourishment of joyful intent is true; this true nourishment is utterly pure and white.
Its aspiration is unsurpassed, its purity is stable, its tranquil bliss is without limit, and its excellence is beyond compare.

The towering radiance shines forth; its illumination extends far and wide, penetrating with clarity. This is the natural mark within the natural state. Thus, it possesses a fundamental source, naturally forming the five lights.

The five lights evolve into nine colors; these nine colors circulate and revolve, undergoing hundreds of thousands of further transformations. This is the spontaneity of Uttarakuru, where things are spontaneously formed from the seven treasures.
Transversely encompassing all things, its radiant essence emerges together with clarity; its beauty is most exquisite and without limit—such is the nature of that land.
Why do you not strive to do good?
Contemplate the spontaneity of the Way, which is manifest in neither high nor low; it penetrates all things without limit, and its resolve is cast into the void.
Why do you not each exert yourselves with diligence?
If one strives to seek it for oneself, one may attain transcendence.
By being reborn in the land of Amitābha Buddha, one cuts across the five evil paths.
These are naturally closed off; ascending to the infinite Way is easy, yet few people do so.
In that land, there is no opposition or contrariety; one is naturally led along by it.
Why not abandon worldly affairs?
By practicing and seeking the Way and its Virtue, one may attain ultimate longevity, with a lifespan that has no limit.
Why do you cling to worldly affairs?
You clamor together in anxiety over impermanence.

The people of this world are shallow and vulgar; they contend over matters that are not urgent, all while dwelling amidst intense evil and extreme suffering. They exert themselves to manage their livelihoods to provide for one another’s survival; whether noble or lowly, rich or poor, old or young, male or female, everyone must alike worry about wealth and property—whether one has it or not is the same for all.
Anxious thoughts are ever-present; one is cowed and distressed, with accumulated reflections and deliberations that cause the mind to run about like a servant, finding no time of peace.

One worries about fields if one has fields, worries about houses if one has houses, worries about oxen if one has oxen, worries about horses if one has horses, worries about the six domestic animals if one has them, and worries about servants and slaves if one has them. Furthermore, regarding clothing, bedding, money, wealth, gold, silver, and precious objects, one worries over them all together.

Reflecting deeply with repeated sighs, one is filled with anxiety, sorrow, and dread, being unexpectedly overwhelmed by calamities—water, fire, thieves, bandits, hostile masters, and creditors—resulting in being drifted away, burned, bound, assaulted, or submerged; thus, the poison of grief and agitation persists without any time of release.

With resentment bound within the breast, one accumulates breath, anger, and fury; illness resides in the chest and abdomen, and sorrow and suffering do not depart. The mind is firm and the will resolute, with no relaxation or relinquishment; perhaps sitting in self-destruction until life ends and the spirit perishes, one departs and abandons all, with no one to follow.
Whether noble or base, wealthy or poor, all possess such anxieties and fears; they labor diligently here, dwelling together with various chills, fevers, and pains.

Those of humble means suffer from poverty and destitution: lacking fields, they worry about wanting fields; lacking houses, they worry about wanting houses; lacking oxen, they worry about wanting oxen; lacking horses, they worry about wanting horses; lacking the six domestic animals, they worry about wanting them; lacking servants or slaves, they worry about wanting them; and lacking clothing, bedding, money, utensils, and food and drink, they likewise worry about wanting these things.
Just when one has obtained one thing less than what was needed, or possesses this deficiency or that, one thinks of attaining equality.
As soon as one has acquired a small amount, it is again bestowed and exhausted; thus suffering arises, and one must seek and search for more once again.

Such useless thoughts cannot be dispelled even with time; body and mind are both exhausted, and one is restless whether sitting or rising. Anxious thoughts follow one another, and the diligent suffering is like this.

A burning heart does not leave behind resentment or solitary anger; it is also bound by various chills and fevers, dwelling together with pain. Sometimes one sits in this state until the end of life or a premature death, yet remains unwilling to perform good deeds or cultivate the Way.

When one's lifespan comes to an end and death arrives, everyone must depart alone and travel far away; as for their destination, whether it be the path of goodness or the path of evil, no one can know.

At times, among the people of this world—fathers and sons, brothers, husbands and wives, family members, and relatives both within and outside the household—who dwell between heaven and earth, they ought to respect and love one another, and not harbor hatred toward one another.
One should give and receive from one another as is appropriate, and should not harbor greed or stinginess.
One’s speech and appearance should be harmonious; do not oppose or act contrary to one another.

Should there happen to be conflict in the mind leading to resentment or anger, even a slight sense of hatred or jealousy harbored with a resentful heart in this life will escalate in future lives until it results in great enmity.
Why is this so? Because even though they do not immediately confront one another with violence at this moment, their sorrow, poison, and pent-up indignation remain bound within their spirits;
these naturally penetrate consciousness and cannot be separated. Thus, they shall inevitably encounter one another in future lives, where they will continue to exact retribution upon each other.

In this world, amidst the midst of desire, a person goes alone, comes alone, dies alone, and is born alone; when one must travel to places of suffering or joy, one must experience it oneself, for there is no one who can take one’s place.

The transformations of good and evil, and the calamitous realms of retribution, lie in wait with prior preparation; one must ascend alone to depart for distant places, and none can see where one has gone.

Good and evil naturally follow one’s deeds as they arise; in the profound and obscure darkness, partings endure for a long time. Paths diverge and there is no set time for meeting again; it is exceedingly difficult to encounter one another once more.
Why not abandon worldly affairs?
While each of you is still strong and healthy, strive diligently to do good; exert yourselves with vigor to seek transcendence from the world, and you shall attain the ultimate long life.
They utterly refuse to seek the Way, yet they wish to wait for it; what joy could there be in that?

"Such people of the world do not believe that performing good deeds brings good results, nor do they believe that practicing the Way brings the attainment of the Way. They do not believe in rebirth after death, nor do they believe that giving alms yields merit and virtue; they simply do not believe in any of these things."

Thinking that it is not so, and that such a thing ultimately does not exist, yet because of this very reason, they see it for themselves; they hear of it from one another in succession, passing it down from predecessor to successor, receiving the remaining instructions of their fathers.

My ancestors and forefathers have never practiced goodness and have fundamentally not pursued the Way. Their bodies were foolish and their spirits dark; their minds were clogged and their intentions closed off. They did not perceive the Great Way, and they utterly lacked the ability to see where people go after death.
No one could know this, nor was there anyone who had seen the path of good and evil, nor anyone to speak of it. Under such circumstances, how could one cultivate good deeds or merit?
Calamities, faults, misfortunes, and punishments each arise competitively; because their manifestations differ, there is nothing strange about them.

As for the way of birth and death, they revolve and continue in succession: sometimes a son weeps for his father, sometimes a father weeps for his son; sometimes a younger brother weeps for his elder brother, sometimes an elder brother weeps for his younger brother; sometimes a wife weeps for her husband, and sometimes a husband weeps for his wife. These roles are inverted and unstable, lacking any constant foundation; all must pass away and cannot be maintained forever.
Though taught and guided by words, those who believe in the Way are few; all must undergo birth and death without end.
Such people as these are blind and ignorant, obstinate and headstrong; they do not believe the words of the scriptures, each desiring only to gratify their own whims.

The mind harbors no reflection; it is deluded by craving and desire, ignorant of the Way and its Virtue, bewildered by anger, and greedily lusting after wealth and beauty. Sitting thus, one fails to attain the Way; one must instead undergo further toil and suffering, being reborn in the most wretched places, never finding rest or peace. How grievous and tragic this pain!

At times, within families—among fathers and sons, brothers, and husbands and wives—their mutual wailing over the principles of life and death leads to ever-increasing longing and attachment. Their grief and anxiety become knotted together, and their bonds of affection continue to entwine them; their minds are gripped by pain as they gaze upon one another with lingering attachment, bound day and night without any time of release.

When taught to contemplate morality, the mind does not become clear; thoughts of favor and sensual desires do not depart; it remains closed, obscured, and shrouded in confusion, such that one is unable to reflect or deliberate.

If one’s mind is upright and resolute in dealing with worldly affairs, and one applies oneself with single-minded diligence to the practice of the Path until the very end, yet fails to attain the Way when life comes to its close and one's lifespan is exhausted, there is nothing that can be done about it.
In general, the clamor and confusion all stem from greed and desire; regarding such phenomena, those who do not understand the Way are many, while those who attain the Way are few.

The world is in a state of frantic haste, with nothing to rely upon for solace. Whether noble or base, superior or inferior, wealthy or poor, male or female, great or small, everyone is preoccupied with their own urgent affairs. They toil and strain their bodies, harboring the poison of murderous intent; their evil vapors are dark and murky, and there is none who does not feel despondent.
They engage in reckless deeds that are rebellious against Heaven and Earth and contrary to the human heart.
While morality itself is not evil, they first comply with such people, allowing them to act as they please; yet before their natural lifespan has reached its end, they suddenly snatch it away.
They fall into the evil realms, enduring toil and suffering for successive lifetimes; they wander through cycles of grief and torment for many thousands of millions of years with no end in sight.
Their pain is beyond words and truly pitiable.
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Ajita and the others:
"O devas, kings, and people, I tell you all: it is because of worldly affairs that people fail to attain the Way; you must reflect upon this thoroughly!"
One should abandon and distance oneself from what is evil, following instead that which is wholesome.

One should hold fast to this and not recklessly commit wrongs, but rather increase the performance of all manner of good deeds. Whether great or small, much or little, the splendors of desire can never be maintained forever; because one must inevitably part from them, there is nothing therein to be truly delighted in.
During the lifetime of the Buddha, those who have faith in and accept the profound words of the Buddhist scriptures, and who practice the Way and its virtue, are all my younger brothers.
Those who wish to newly study the precepts of the Buddhist scriptures are all my disciples.

Those who wish to leave their bodies behind, depart from their homes, renounce their wives and children, sever ties with wealth and beauty, and desire to become śramaṇas and bhikṣus for the sake of the Buddha—all such persons are my sons and grandsons.

This world is extremely difficult to encounter; those who wish to be born in the land of Amitābha Buddha shall attain wisdom and valor and be respected by the multitude. You must not follow your own whims and thereby violate the sutras and precepts, falling behind others.
Should you have any doubts or fail to understand the sutras, come forward again to question the Buddha, and I shall explain them for you.
The Bodhisattva Ajita knelt with palms joined and said:
"The Buddha’s majestic power is most venerable, and the sutras he has spoken are excellent and sublime.
As we have listened to the words of the sutra, they have all penetrated our minds."
The people of the world are indeed as the Buddha has said, without any difference.

Now the Buddha, out of compassion for us, has revealed the Great Way and taught the path of rebirth; our ears and eyes have become clear and sharp, and we shall forever attain liberation, as if we were born anew today.
Among us who have listened to the words of the Buddha’s sutras, there are none whose compassionate hearts do not leap with joy and find liberation.
Furthermore, all the devas, kings, common people, and even the wriggling insects and crawling creatures receive his grace; there is none among them who is not delivered from sorrow and suffering.
The Buddha’s words, teachings, and precepts are profoundly good, infinite and bottomless.

That which is seen and known by the Buddha’s wisdom—matters of the eight directions, above and below, past, future, and present—is unsurpassed, without inferiority, boundless, and limitless; such a Buddha is extremely difficult to encounter and hear.

That we have been compared by the Buddha to those who possess a compassionate heart, and that we have been enabled to attain liberation, is entirely due to the diligent suffering, study, and spiritual clarity he achieved while seeking the Way in his previous lives.
His benevolence and virtue cover all universally; the merit he practices brings forth majestic marks and blessings so lofty that his radiance shines through, penetrating the infinite void.
He enters into Nirvana, teaching and mastering the scriptures, establishing majestic authority and dissolving delusions.
Transforming the eight directions, above and below, infinitely and boundlessly, the Buddha serves as the supreme teacher and law, far surpassing all sages; none can equal the Buddha.
As the teacher for the devas, emperors, and people of the eight directions, above and below, he causes both the great and the small to attain the Way according to their hearts' desires and vows.
"Now that we have been able to meet the Buddha and hear the voice of Amitābha Buddha, we are filled with great joy; there is not one among us who has not attained wisdom and clarity."
The Buddha told Bodhisattva Ajita:
"If you say this, it is indeed so.
If there is one who possesses a heart of loving-kindness toward the Buddha, they will rejoice greatly and should truly practice mindfulness of the Buddha."
After a long time in this world, there is once again a Buddha.
Now, I have appeared as a Buddha in this world of suffering; the sutras and teachings I have brought forth provide thorough instruction and sever all doubts.
With a focused mind and upright conduct, he uproots all cravings and severs the roots of all evils.
His movements are unhindered as he presides over and masters wisdom.
He grasps the essential principles that govern the inner and outer aspects of all paths.
"It is clearly illuminated, opening the vision of the five paths and decisively establishing the way of birth-and-death and *nirvāṇa*.
The Buddha said:

"Since incalculable *kalpas* ago—indeed, for an immeasurable number of *kalpas*—you have practiced the path of the Bodhisattva, desiring to deliver all devas, humans, and even the wriggling insects; this has already been for a very long time."
The number of people who have attained the Way and crossed over is infinite; those who have reached the path of Nirvana are likewise infinite.

You all—whether among the gods of the eight directions and the zenith and nadir, kings, emperors, and commoners, or bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās—have, throughout your past lives since incalculable kalpas, transmigrated through these five realms of existence. Amidst death and birth, you have sighed and lamented, weeping for one another; you have harbored mutual greed and longing, suffering from grief, anxiety, and distress, enduring pains that are beyond description.

To this day, birth and death have continued without end; that you have now met and encountered the Buddha together is truly a most joyful and auspicious occasion. It is a great blessing to hear the voice of Amitābha Buddha, and I join you all in your joy.

One may also grow weary of the pains and itchings of birth and death: at the time of birth, it is extremely painful, extremely bitter, and extremely extreme; as one grows to adulthood, it is likewise bitter and extreme; at the time of death, it is likewise painful, bitter, and extreme. It is a place of foul stench and impurity, utterly devoid of anything clean or desirable.
The Buddha therefore tells you all this: you yourselves must also resolve to sever the foul-smelling, impure secretions.
You should also rectify your minds and align your bodies, further performing all manner of wholesome deeds.
Thereupon, they constantly maintain rectitude both internally and externally, purify their bodies, and wash away the defilements of the mind.
They mutually restrain themselves, ensuring that their inner intentions and outer conduct correspond, and that their words and deeds are loyal and trustworthy.

If a person can liberate themselves, assist one another in succession, uproot all craving and desire, maintain a refined spirit and utmost sincerity, and pursue their vows without wavering, thereby establishing the root of the path to goodness—then though they undergo diligent austerity for a lifetime, it is but a mere moment.

If one performs good deeds in this life, one will be reborn in the Land of Amitābha Buddha in a future life, where happiness is boundless and one shall forever be united with the brilliance of the Way and its Virtue.

Thus, by steadfastly maintaining these wholesome qualities, one shall forever depart from the anxieties and afflictions of the evil realms, uproot the various evils that are the source of suffering, and sever all cravings and attachments.

In the Land of Amitābha Buddha, one attains eternal life; there are no sensations of pain or itching, nor are there any places of foul odors. Furthermore, there is no toil or suffering, nor are there lust, anger, or delusion, and there is no anxiety, grief, or mental torment.

Born in the land of Amitābha Buddha, if you wish your lifespan to last for one kalpa, ten kalpas, a hundred kalpas, a thousand kalpas, or ten billion kalpas—or if you desire to dwell for an incalculable number of kalpas beyond measure—you may have it as you please; all this can be obtained according to your own will.
Whether they desire food or not, let their wills be as they wish; all things are spontaneously present and can be obtained.
Next, regarding the path to Nirvana, each shall individually and with clarity seek it out.

If you have a desire or aspiration, do not harbor doubt or regret in your heart. Those who wish to be reborn there must not sit idly by their transgressions; they shall be exiled for five hundred years within a city of the seven treasures that exists naturally on the borders of Amitābha Buddha’s realm.
The Bodhisattva Ajita said:

"Having received the Buddha’s solemn and weighty instruction, we shall all strive with single-minded diligence to seek it out; we pray that you permit us to carry it out, for we dare not harbor doubt or negligence."
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Ajita and the others:
"If you, in this world, are able to restrain your own minds, rectify your intentions, and refrain from committing evil with your bodies, this constitutes great virtue and goodness."
There is a class of beings who are peerless throughout the eight directions and the zenith and nadir. Why is this?

Because in the countless Buddha-fields of the eight directions and the zenith and nadir, the devas and humans all spontaneously perform good deeds and do not commit great evils; they are easy to teach and transform.

Now, as I have become a Buddha in this world, I act as a Buddha amidst the five evils, the five pains, and the five burnings; this is my most arduous task. I instruct the people, causing them to abandon the five evils, to eliminate the five pains, and to put away the five burnings. I subdue and transform their minds, leading them to uphold the five virtues so that they may attain merit, transcend the world, and reach the path of long life and Nirvana.
The Buddha said:
“What are the five evils?
What are the five sufferings?”
What are the five that burn within?
What are the means to digest the five evils and attain the five virtues?
And what are the means to maintain the five virtues, thereby attaining the merit, long life, and the path to nirvāṇa that transcends the world?
The Buddha said:
"As for the first evil:

from the devas and human beings down to birds, beasts, and all classes of wriggling and crawling creatures, they desire to commit various evils; the strong subjugate the weak and mutually oppress one another, killing and wounding each other, and devouring one another."

Not knowing how to perform good deeds, they commit evil and rebellious acts contrary to the Way, thereby receiving calamities and punishments. This is the natural law of the Way: one must proceed toward the divine spirits who record such deeds; having committed them, there is no pardon, and the consequences continue in succession.

Thus, there are those who are poor, lowly, beggars, and solitary; likewise, there are those who are deaf, blind, mute, foolish, and wicked; and below these, there are those who are physically infirm, insane, or otherwise deficient.

Therefore, those who possess honor and status, nobility and wealth, superior talent, clarity and insight, wisdom, and courage—all these are the result of their having performed good deeds, practiced compassion and filial piety, and bestowed gifts with benevolence in their previous lives.

Consequently, when faced with official affairs, royal law, and imprisonment, they refuse to act with fear and caution; thus they commit evils that bring them under the law, receiving reprimands and heavy punishments that lead to extreme suffering, making it difficult for them to seek liberation or find deliverance.

That which exists in this life is the present; when one’s lifespan ends, one enters into the profound darkness of that place and receives a body to be born again, which is like the severe suffering of the king’s law and the most extreme punishments.

Therefore, there are those who naturally fall into the realms of hell, animals, hungry ghosts, and the class of crawling and flying insects; they undergo transformations of physical form, changing their evil ways for better paths, while their lifespans—whether long or short—and their spirits and consciousnesses naturally enter these destinies to receive forms and dwell within wombs.
When one encounters these conditions alone or when they arise together through mutual association, they revolve in a cycle of retribution and compensation, returning back to the source.
As long as the calamities, evils, misfortunes, and punishments have not been fully exhausted, one shall ultimately never escape them.
They revolve within it through successive lifetimes and kalpas with no time of escape; liberation is difficult to attain, and the suffering is beyond description.

Such is the natural state between heaven and earth: although things do not manifest suddenly or abruptly at any given moment, they simply follow the way of nature, wherein all good and evil must find their retribution.
This constitutes one great evil, one agony, and one burning.
Such is the diligent suffering, the sorrowful torment, and the lamentation; it is comparable to a fierce fire breaking out and burning a person's body.

If a person can, within this state, unify their mind to control their intentions, rectify their body to correct their conduct, and alone perform all manner of good while refraining from all evil, they will personally attain liberation and its blessings and virtues; they shall obtain long life, transcend the world, ascend to heaven, and reach the path of Nirvana—this is called the first great good.
The Buddha said:
"As for those two evils:

among the world's emperors, high officials, and common people—fathers and sons, brothers, family members, and husbands and wives—there is almost no sense of righteousness or principle. They do not follow correct commands; they are extravagant, lustful, and arrogant. Each desires only to satisfy their own whims and indulge their hearts at will, mutually deceiving and provoking one another, without having the slightest fear of death."

Their hearts and mouths differ; their words and thoughts lack sincerity. They are sycophantic, unfaithful, and fawning, employing clever and artful speech. Their conduct lacks integrity, and they harbor mutual jealousy and hatred, repeatedly slandering one another and ensnaring others in wrongful injustice.

The sovereign is not enlightened and does not examine with discernment, yet he appoints his subordinates. These subordinates exist while treading upon the bounds of propriety, yet they know how to manifest their influence; though occupying positions of authority, they are not upright. Being manipulated by them, they recklessly harm the loyal, the good, and the virtuous. This does not accord with the will of Heaven and is profoundly contrary to the Way.

Ministers deceive their sovereigns, sons deceive their fathers, younger brothers deceive their elder brothers, and wives deceive their husbands; members of the household, those within and without, and acquaintances all engage in mutual litigation, each harboring greed and lust, with hearts poisoned by malice and anger, blinded by ignorance and folly, yet desiring only to increase [their own gains].
There is no distinction of noble or base, superior or inferior; there is no male, no female, no great, and no small. Their minds are all alike in their desire to enrich themselves.

They ruin their families and bring about their own destruction, heedless of what lies before or behind them; because of them, their households and kinsmen sit and witness the destruction of their clans.

At times, among those known to them—whether relatives, friends, or acquaintances within and outside the household, or even the ignorant commoners and country folk of their villages and market towns—they become further entangled in mutual interests and harms.

They contend over wealth, engage in litigation, and give rise to enmity through anger; they continue to dispute over victory and defeat, and being stingy with their riches, they burn with anxiety, refusing to practice generosity.
One prays and prays, guarding one's affections and cherishing what is grasped; thus, while sitting in contemplation, the mind is weary and the body suffers.
In this way, until the very end, there is nothing upon which to rely; one comes alone and departs alone, with not a single follower.

Regarding the blessings and misfortunes, merits and calamities, or punishments that follow one’s life—whether leading to rebirth in places of joy or entry into realms of bitter suffering—it is only then that one regrets; what use will it be to try to remedy it then?

At times, people of the world possess foolish minds and little wisdom; seeing what is good, they slander it and resent it, refusing to admire or emulate it. They desire only to act perversely and unrighteously, seeking only to steal while constantly harboring poisonous intentions. Desiring to obtain the wealth of others to provide for themselves, they squander it until it is exhausted, only to seek more once again.
With a perverse mind and abnormality, one alone feels terror and dread toward those with form; failing to deliberate on matters when the time comes, one only regrets them once they have arrived.
In this present life, one naturally moves toward the prisons of high officials and suffers their calamities and retributions.

Those in this world who are impoverished, beggars, or solitary, do so solely because in their past lives they did not believe in the Way and its Virtue and were unwilling to perform good deeds; having committed evil in this life, they are registered as separate from the celestial deities and, at the end of their lives, enter the evil realms.

Consequently, there are natural hells, as well as the realms of birds, beasts, hungry ghosts, and all classes of crawling and flying insects; transmigrating within these states through successive lifetimes and kalpas without any prospect of escape, it is difficult to attain liberation, and the suffering is beyond words.
These are the two great evils, the two pains, and the two burnings.
Such diligent suffering is like a fire breaking out that burns more fiercely than a person's own body.

If a person can, within this midst, single-mindedly restrain their thoughts, align their body, and rectify their conduct, performing only various good deeds and committing no evil, they alone shall attain liberation and obtain merit; they may achieve longevity, transcend the world to ascend to heaven, and realize the path of Nirvāṇa—these are the two great virtues.
The Buddha said:
"As for those three evils:
all people of the world live as transient guests, mutually dependent upon one another, dwelling together between heaven and earth; as for their years of life, none can endure for many years."

There are noble and wealthy elders, wise and virtuous people; below them, there are the poor, lowly, frail, and foolish; and among them, there are those of ill character who harbor poisonous thoughts, whose bodies and minds are not upright, and who constantly dwell on lewdness until it fills their chests. Their desires and passions entwine so that they find no peace whether sitting or rising;
with greedy minds and stingy hearts, they crave to obtain things at will, casting covetous glances at subtle forms and manifesting wicked, lewd attitudes.
There were wives who detested and loathed their husbands, entering and leaving at will to engage in illicit affairs; they used the family's possessions to support their misconduct.

They gathered for feasts and meals solely to commit evil, raising armies and acting as bandits to besiege cities and fight in battles; they committed robbery, murder, and highway robbery, seizing by force in a manner that defied all morality.
They seize the property of others through theft and stealth, refusing to engage in productive livelihoods; they are unwilling to do what ought to be done.

With malicious intent directed outward, they cannot focus on their work; they desire to complete their tasks but fear intimidation by powerful forces. They carry back what they have acquired to provide for their households, living together in mutual dependence.
Indulging their hearts and seeking pleasure, they engage in excessive revelry and commit adultery with the wives of others.

They show no regard for kinship, nor do they avoid those who are honorable, elders, or seniors; consequently, the masses detest them, and both within and outside the household, everyone suffers from and is incensed by them.
Furthermore, they do not fear the laws and edicts of the local authorities, nor do they avoid recording their transgressions.

Such evils naturally result in imprisonment; the sun and moon illuminate their consciousness, and the divine spirits take note and record them. Consequently, there are natural hells (*niraya*), as well as the realms of birds, beasts, hungry ghosts (*preta*), and all classes of crawling and flying insects. They transmigrate within these states through successive lives and across kalpas with no foreseeable end, finding liberation difficult to attain—a suffering beyond description.
These are the three great evils, the three pains, and the three burnings.
Such is the diligent suffering, comparable to a fire breaking out that burns a person's body.

If a person can, within this state, single-mindedly restrain their thoughts, align their body, and rectify their conduct—acting alone in various virtues and committing no manifold evils—they will alone attain liberation and obtain its merit; they may achieve long life, transcend the world, ascend to heaven, and reach the Way of Nirvana. These are the three great virtues.
The Buddha said:
"As for those four evils:
people are unable to perform good deeds; they destroy one another and, moreover, instruct each other to commit various evils together."

The master incites others merely to engage in double-tongued speech, harsh words, abuse, and lying; they harbor mutual jealousy and incite strife, detesting and envying virtuous people, ruining the worthy and good, and finding pleasure in such conduct from the sidelines.

Furthermore, they are unfilial and fail to provide for their parents; they treat their teachers, friends, and spiritual mentors with contempt; lacking faith, they find it difficult to attain sincerity.

Arrogant and self-important, they consider themselves noble and possessed of the Way; they act with reckless violence, wielding power and influence to oppress and exploit others, unable to recognize their own faults.
Committing evil without shame or remorse, they consider themselves stubborn and strong, desiring that others serve and revere them.

Furthermore, they do not stand in awe of Heaven, Earth, the spirits, the sun, or the moon; nor can they be taught to do good, nor can they be transformed or subdued, for they remain obstinate and arrogant, always acting as they please.
Furthermore, he was devoid of any sense of sorrow or grief, nor did he know the meaning of fear.
His arrogance was such that even the celestial deities took note of him.
However, owing to the merit he had accumulated through his past lives, a small amount of goodness supported, sustained, and protected him.
In this life, one’s evil deeds are exhausted, all virtues depart day by day, and one sees evil pursuing them.

Standing alone and empty with nothing left to rely upon, one undergoes heavy calamities and retributions. As the end of one’s lifespan approaches, a multitude of evils surround and return; naturally pressing and urgent, they must pursue one without respite. Naturally, amidst the convergence of manifold evils, one suddenly becomes exhausted.
