Their names are recorded in the registers of the divine spirits; when their misfortunes and transgressions draw them together and they encounter one another, they naturally proceed to receive retribution and punishment. Their bodies and minds are shattered, and their spirits and forms suffer extreme agony from which there is no escape; they can only press forward into the fiery cauldrons.
At such a time, what benefit would repentance bring? What could possibly be reached by it?

The Way of Heaven is spontaneous and cannot be faltered; therefore, there exist the natural hells, the realms of birds and beasts, the hungry ghosts (*preta*), and the wriggling insects and crawling creatures. One revolves within these states through successive lifetimes and kalpas with no prospect of escape; liberation is difficult to attain, and the suffering is beyond description.
These are the four great evils, the four afflictions, and the four burnings.
Such is the diligent suffering, comparable to a fire breaking out and burning a person's body.

If a person can, within this state, single-mindedly restrain their thoughts, align their body, and rectify their conduct—acting alone in all that is good and committing no evil—then they alone shall attain liberation and obtain merit; they may achieve long life, transcend the world, ascend to heaven, and realize the path of Nirvāṇa.
"These are the four great virtues.
The Buddha said:
"As for the five evils:"

The people of this world loiter about indolently; they are unwilling to perform good deeds and do not think of managing their livelihoods. Their wives and children suffer from hunger and cold, as do their parents. When one wishes to reprimand and instruct one's son, the son harbors malice; he glares with eyes of wrath and responds with angry words, refusing to obey. His defiance and perversity exceed even that of a common rustic; he is like an enemy, and it would be better to have no son at all than such a one.
He recklessly and extensively borrowed from others, causing universal resentment and weariness; moreover, he had no intention whatsoever of repaying his debts.

Being utterly impoverished and destitute, he could obtain nothing further, yet he continued to manipulate sounds for profit and indulge in dissipation. Habituated to obtaining things through deceit, he used them for his own distribution and relief without fearing prohibitions. His eating and drinking were excessive; he was addicted to wine and savory delicacies. His comings and goings lacked any regular measure, and he was coarse, arrogant, and intrusive, showing no regard for human feelings and sighing loudly with unrestrained force.
When they see others who are joyful, they harbor hatred, envy, and anger; lacking both righteousness and propriety, they follow their own arbitrary notions and cannot be admonished or enlightened.

Furthermore, they do not worry about the welfare of their parents, wives, or children, nor do they consider repaying the kindness of their parents, nor do they think of the benevolence of their teachers.
Their minds constantly contemplate evil, their mouths constantly speak evil, and their bodies constantly perform evil.

Day after day they achieve nothing; they do not believe in the Way and its Virtue, nor do they believe in the existence of the wise sages of old. They do not believe that practicing goodness constitutes the Way by which one may attain deliverance from the world, nor do they believe that there is a Buddha in this world.

He desires to kill arhats, to fight against the community of bhikṣus, and constantly seeks to kill people—desiring to kill his father, mother, elder brother, younger brother, wife, children, kinsmen, and friends.
Toward their parents, brothers, wives, children, kinsmen, and friends, they harbor hatred and wish for them to die;
they do not believe the words of the Buddhist scriptures, nor do they believe that human life ends in death and is reborn in a future world.
They do not believe that performing good brings good, nor that performing evil brings evil.

Such people—both men and women—are likewise in their hearts and minds rebellious and perverse; they are deluded by ignorance, prone to anger and sensual desire, and devoid of discernment. Yet they are self-satisfied, considering themselves virtuous and regarding themselves as possessing great wisdom.

They do not know whence they have come nor where their births and deaths will lead; they refuse to practice filial piety and instead act with malice and rebellion against Heaven and Earth. Amidst these conditions, they hope for mere luck and fortune, desiring long life and invoking immortality; yet they must inevitably return to the cycle of birth and death and the path of toil, suffering, and the retribution of good and evil deeds. For the evils committed by their own bodies, they shall fall into the various realms of existence and find no liberation.

Furthermore, they cannot be subdued or transformed to perform wholesome deeds; even when taught and exhorted with a compassionate heart to open them to the suffering of death, and told that there is such a thing as the destination of good and evil, they still do not believe it.
Yet, though one exerts great effort in both heart and speech, desiring to deliver and liberate them, it brings no benefit to those people.

Their minds remain blocked and their thoughts find no resolution; when their great life-force is about to end, they feel regret at that very moment. Once it is too late, what can be done by their subsequent remorse?
If one does not plan to perform good deeds in advance, what benefit is there when facing one's final end?

Within the realm of heaven and earth, the five paths are each distinct; vast, profound, and immense, they flow on like a great flood. Beings pass these states on to one another, experiencing the bitterness and pain of their good and evil deeds, which they must bear themselves with no one to take their place.

The Way is spontaneous; it follows wherever one acts, pursuing the destiny of one's birth without allowing for negligence or abandonment. When good people practice goodness and cultivate compassion and filial piety, they proceed from joy to joy, and from illumination to illumination.
When evil persons commit evil deeds, they follow from suffering to darkness.
Who is able to know this?
Only the Buddha perceives and knows it alone.
When teaching the people, those who believe and trust are few; birth and death do not cease, and the evil realms remain uninterrupted. Thus, the ways of the world cannot be fully described:

there are the natural hells (*niraya*), as well as the realms of birds and beasts, hungry ghosts (*preta*), and all crawling and flying insects. They revolve within these states through successive lives and kalpas with no time of escape; liberation is difficult to attain, and the suffering is beyond words.
These are the five great evils, the five pains, and the five burnings.
To undergo such diligent suffering is like a fire breaking out that burns a person’s body.

If a person can, within this state, single-mindedly restrain their thoughts, align their body with upright conduct, ensure their words match their deeds, act with ultimate sincerity, speak as they intend, and remain consistent in heart and mouth, performing only various good deeds and committing no evil, then that person alone shall attain liberation and obtain its merit; they may achieve long life, transcend the world, ascend to heaven, and realize the path of Nirvana.
"These are the five great evils.
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Ajita and the others:
"I have told you all that the five evils of this world involve such diligent suffering; they give rise to the five pains and the five burnings, which arise from one another in succession."

The people of the world are unwilling to do good and desire to commit various evils; those who dare to transgress by committing such evil deeds shall all naturally and inevitably undergo the experience of entering the evil realms.

Or perhaps they have already been afflicted by the calamities of disease in this life, yet they cannot attain liberation from birth and death; they show themselves to the multitude, but when their lives end, they enter into the ultimate great suffering, grief, and bitter torment. They are consumed within themselves and burn one another down, until finally they become enemies who wound and kill each other. From these minor beginnings, they reach the height of great distress and agony—all arising from greed for wealth and beauty, refusing to practice patience or generosity, desiring only their own pleasure, and seeking a reputation for prowess regardless of right or wrong.
Driven by ignorance and desire, they follow their own mental imaginings and can no longer recover [their original state]; resentment knots within their chests.
Bound by wealth and sensual pleasures, they find no liberation and know no contentment; they enrich themselves and strive for desire without any sense of reflection or restraint.
While enjoying wealth, status, and splendor, one may endure insults and fail to practice charity or do good; yet before long, such power vanishes and one is scorched by an ill reputation.
The body sits in toil and hardship until it becomes exceedingly severe; thus one is naturally pursued by suffering without any possibility of release.

When the king’s laws are extended, they naturally constrain and elevate, with superiors and subordinates acting in harmony; yet within this net and its governing framework, the solitary and the trembling find themselves ensnared—how painful and lamentable this has been throughout antiquity and the present!
"They possess no righteous principle and do not know the Right Path.
The Buddha spoke to the Bodhisattva Ajita and the others:

"If there are such beings in the world, all Buddhas will take pity on them with compassion; through their majestic spiritual power, they shall subdue and move them, causing all their evil deeds to be digested and dissolved, so that they may abandon evil, turn toward goodness, and cast away their deluded thoughts."
They uphold the sutras and precepts, receiving them all without exception; they practice the teachings of the sutras, never daring to transgress or lose them.
They attain the path of world-transcending non-action and nirvana, which is blissful, virtuous, and supreme joy.
The Buddha said:
"You gods, emperors, people, and those of future generations, having obtained the words of the Buddha’s sutras, should contemplate them deeply.

You should be able to rectify your own minds and align your conduct within them. May your sovereigns practice goodness and lead their subjects through transformation and restraint; may they instruct the masses and issue mutual exhortations, so that together you may do good and mutually deliver one another."

Each person shall steadfastly maintain compassion and pity, never flagging until the end of their lives; they shall honor the sages and respect their parents, extending profound and universal love, and shall not dare to violate or neglect the teachings and commands of the Buddha.

One should be concerned with the path of transcending the world and attaining *nirvāṇa*; one should be concerned with severing the cycle of birth and death and its painful sensations, and uprooting the fundamental source of evil; one should be concerned with cutting off the paths of suffering for those in the hells, as animals, as hungry ghosts (*preta*), and as all crawling and flying insects.
"When the Buddha is in the world, you must firmly uphold the Way of the Sūtras and dare not violate or lose it.
The Buddha said:
"If you all must believe, what is the foremost urgency?"

One should straighten one's own body; one should straighten one's own mind; one should straighten one's own eyes; one should straighten one's own ears; one should straighten one's own nose; one should straighten one's own mouth; one should straighten one's own hands; one should straighten one's own feet. One should be able to restrain oneself and not act recklessly. With body and mind pure and clean, acting in complete harmony, one should exercise self-restraint both internally and externally, and must not follow after sensual desires.
Do not commit any evil; let your speech and countenance be harmonious, and let your bodily conduct be focused.
In walking, sitting, and rising, let all your actions be composed.
In whatever task you undertake, you should first deliberate upon it thoroughly and plan it well.
One should gauge one's own abilities and observe the proper measure, acting with stability and deliberation.

If one acts with haste, failing to plan thoroughly and acting without careful attention, one will squander one's efforts; subsequent regret and failure will follow, leading to fruitless toil and the loss of oneself.
"Through utmost sincerity, loyalty, and faithfulness, one attains the Way and transcends [the world].
The Buddha said:

"If you all further perform various good deeds therein, bestowing kindness and practicing virtue, and are able not to transgress the prohibitions of the Way—exercising patience, diligence, single-mindedness, and wisdom, and successively teaching and transforming one another to cultivate goodness and virtue."

If one practices this sutra-dharma with single-minded compassion and observes the pure precepts for a single day and night, it is superior to performing good deeds for a hundred years in the land of Amitābha Buddha.

Why is this? Because in the land of Amitābha Buddha, all is accumulated through merit and manifold goodness; it is unconditioned and spontaneous, fulfilling whatever one seeks, and there is not a single evil as small as a hair.
The Buddha said, "In this regard,
the merit of one who performs wholesome deeds for ten days and ten nights surpasses that of the people in the Buddha-lands of other directions who perform wholesome deeds for a thousand years."

Why is this? In the Buddha-lands of other directions, all practice goodness; those who do good are many, while those who commit evil are few. All things there are spontaneous; one does not need to strive to seek them, for they are obtained of their own accord.
In this world, those who do evil are many, while those who perform good deeds are few; they do not practice with diligence and thus cannot achieve realization.
It is only because worldly people can cultivate themselves with integrity, perform good deeds, and seek the Way with a sincere heart that they are able to attain such results!

In this world there is nothing that arises spontaneously; unable to provide for oneself, one must go out to seek and strive through diligent toil to sustain one's life. People deceive and exploit one another, using guile to judge the good and the bad, and having obtained wealth and goods, they return them to their wives and children, yet they consume them with poisonous labor, causing suffering to both mind and body.
Thus, until the very end, his mind was not focused; he was restless and uneasy.
It is only because a person can bring themselves to tranquility and cultivate the virtue of diligent progress toward the good that such a state is possible!
The Buddha said:

"I have compassion for you all, as well as for the devas, kings, and the people; I instruct you all to perform various good deeds and not to commit any evils, bestowing upon you the Way according to each person's capacity."

They all received and practiced these teachings and admonitions; thus, the ruler led by example toward goodness, instructing his ministers, the father his son, the elder brother his younger brother, and the husband his wife. Within the household, relatives and friends exhorted one another to perform good deeds as the Way, to revere the sutras and uphold the precepts. Each maintained their integrity with superiors and subordinates mutually restraining one another. Whether noble or humble, male or female, all observed the fasts and precepts with purity, rejoicing in harmony, righteousness, benevolence, and filial piety, binding themselves to one another through mutual self-restraint.

If there are those who obtain the words of the Buddha’s sutras and maintain them all in mind, yet commit transgressions by acting contrary to what they should do, they should immediately repent for their past evils and turn toward the good. Abandoning the heterodox for the orthodox, changing in the evening what was heard in the morning, they uphold the sutras and precepts with such intensity as a fool finding a treasure.

In whatever kingdoms and states the Buddha traveled, he would immediately bestow upon them the sutras and precepts. Among the devas, the sun, moon, stars, and various spirits; the kings, ministers, high officials, and common people; and the dragons, ghosts, spirits, hell-beings, birds, beasts, hungry ghosts, and all classes of crawling and flying insects—there were none whose compassionate hearts were not opened and liberated. They all served him with reverence, prostrating themselves before the Buddha to receive the Way of the sutras, and they upheld and practiced them accordingly.

If you immediately reform and transform yourself toward goodness, observing the fasts and precepts with refined contemplation to purify yourself through cleansing, aligning your mind and rectifying your conduct while maintaining solemn reverence in your station, instructing and leading the multitude to do good, upholding the prohibitions of the Way, and ensuring that your words and commands are upright.
A minister serves his sovereign with filial piety and loyalty, receiving his commands with integrity and not daring to disobey or betray them.

Between father and son, words and commands are received with filial obedience. Among brothers, husband and wife, kinsmen, and friends, those above and below issue commands to one another, responding with harmonious speech and rational accord.
The honorable and the humble, the great and the small, will treat one another with mutual respect and service; they will act according to propriety and righteousness without mutual betrayal.

None will fail to reform their past ways and cultivate themselves for the future, purifying their minds and transforming their conduct so that both their inner thoughts and outward appearances are upright. Thus, they will naturally perform good deeds and attain whatever they wish for immediately.
All are well-versed in the Way of spontaneous transformation and subduing.
If one seeks immortality, one may attain longevity;
if one seeks to transcend the world, one may attain the Way of Nirvana.
The Buddha said:
“The Buddha’s majestic spiritual power is honored and his virtue is profound; there is nothing he does not deliver through the eradication of evil and the transformation toward good.
Now that I have appeared in the world, remaining amidst this wickedness, I act as a Buddha within this suffering age, teaching, exhorting, and guiding with compassion and pity.”
The devas, emperors, ministers, attendants, high officials, and the common people—all, according to their respective hearts' wishes and inclinations, were caused to attain the Way.

Wherever the Buddha traveled—through the provinces, kingdoms, counties, towns, villages, hamlets, and marketplaces—all places became abundant and fertile; the world was at peace, the sun and moon shone with doubled brilliance, wind and rain fell in their proper seasons, and the people lived in tranquility.
The strong do not oppress the weak; each finds their proper place. There are no years of famine or pestilence, and none suffer from illness or emaciation.
Weapons of war are not raised; the land is free of thieves and bandits. There are no grievances or injustices, and no one is subjected to imprisonment.

The ruler, ministers, and the people were all filled with joy and leaped for gladness; with loyalty, compassion, and utmost sincerity, each maintained their integrity and guarded their own state, living in harmony, filial piety, and universal delight.
There were those who bestowed kindness and virtue upon one another; their hearts were joyful, and they all respected, loved, yielded to, and showed humility toward one another.
From beginning to end, they served each other with ritual propriety and reverence, like father and son, like elder and younger brother; there were none who were not benevolent and virtuous.
"Harmonious and compliant with propriety, they are entirely free from conflict; their joy and goodness are boundless.
The Buddha said:

"I pity you all and desire to deliver you, thinking of you even more intensely than a parent thinks of a child. Now, among the devas, emperors, and people of the eight directions and the zenith and nadir, as well as the wriggling and crawling creatures, those who obtain the sutras and precepts of the Buddha and practice the Buddhist Way shall all attain clear wisdom and have their minds fully opened and liberated. There shall be none who do not transcend and be released from sorrow and suffering."

Now that I have become a Buddha, while dwelling amidst the five evils, the five pains, and the five burnings, I subdue and transform the five evils, eliminate and exhaust the five pains, and utterly extinguish the five burnings.

By using the good to attack the evil, one uproots poisonous suffering and enables the attainment of the five paths; one enables the attainment of the five wholesome virtues that are bright and excellent, so that the burning of evil does not arise.

After my parinirvāṇa, when the sutras and the Way gradually become severed, people will become sycophantic and deceitful, increasingly committing various evils and no longer performing good deeds. The five burnings will arise again, and the five agonizing pains will be as severe as before; they will naturally recur, and after a long time they will grow even more intense beyond all description.
"I have merely taught you this minor path.
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Ajita and the others:
"Each of you should contemplate and uphold it, teaching and exhorting one another in turn, so that none dare to transgress the Dharma of the Buddha’s sutras."
The Bodhisattva Ajita knelt with palms joined and said:
“The record of the Buddha-way is exceedingly painful.
The evils committed by the people of the world are as severe as this.”

The Buddha, out of universal compassion, delivers them all; they all say that having received the Buddha’s profound instruction, they request to teach one another in succession, not daring to commit any transgression.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Out of pity for you all, I shall cause you to see Amitābha Buddha, as well as the lands where the bodhisattvas and arhats dwell."
"If you wish to see them?
Ānanda was immediately filled with great joy; kneeling with palms joined, he said, "I wish to see them all."
The Buddha said:
"If you rise, put on your kashaya robe again and bow facing west toward the place where the sun sets. Pay homage to Amitābha Buddha by placing your head upon the ground and say:
'Namo Amitābha Tathāgata.'"
Ānanda said, “Yes! I accept your instruction.”
He immediately rose, adjusted his *kāṣāya*, and bowed toward the west; facing the place where the sun had set, he prostrated before Amitābha Buddha, placing his head upon the ground and saying:
"Namo Amitābha Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha."
Before Ānanda had risen, Amitābha Buddha immediately emitted a great radiance of majestic spiritual power, which pervaded the countless buddha-lands in the eight directions, above, and below.
All the countless worlds and heavens were immediately shaken with a great trembling.

In all those countless worlds and heavens, including the Mount Sumerus and the jewel-adorned Mahāsumeru mountains, as well as the various worlds—both great realms and small realms—the great hells and small hells therein, and the dark places of mountains, forests, streams, and valleys, were all suddenly filled with great radiance and completely opened wide.

At that moment, Ānanda, all the bodhisattvas, arhats, devas, emperors, and common people, having beheld Amitābha Buddha and the land of the bodhisattvas and arhats adorned with the seven treasures, were filled with great joy and leaped for gladness. They all rose, prostrated themselves before Amitābha Buddha, touching their heads to the ground, and all cried out:
"Namo Amitābha Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha!"

By the power of the radiance and majestic spiritual authority emitted from the land of Amitābha Buddha, all the countless devas, humans, and even the crawling and flying insects all behold the light of Amitābha Buddha; there is none among them who does not feel compassion in their hearts and rejoice.

All those in the hells, among the beasts, or as hungry ghosts, and all who dwell in places of torment and diligent suffering, immediately find rest and cease their punishment; there is none who is not liberated from sorrow and pain.

All who were blind immediately gained sight; all who were deaf immediately gained hearing; all who were mute immediately became able to speak; all who were hunchbacked immediately straightened; all who were lame, crippled, or halting immediately began to run; all who were ill immediately recovered and rose up; all who were weak immediately became strong and healthy; all who were foolish immediately became wise; all who were lustful all practiced the holy life (*brahmacarya*); all who were angry all became compassionate in mind and performed good deeds; and for all who were afflicted by poison, the poison ceased to take effect.
The bells, stone chimes, lutes, zithers, harps, and various musical instruments all produced the five musical notes spontaneously without being struck.
The jeweled bracelets of the women all made sounds of their own accord, and the hundred birds and beasts all cried out piteously on their own.
At that time, there were none who did not rejoice with great delight and attain deliverance.

Immediately, the devas and people from the lands of all the Buddhas brought celestial flowers and incense down to the earth; in the midst of the void, they all made offerings, scattering them upon the various Buddhas and upon Amitābha Buddha.
The various devas each together performed ten thousand kinds of spontaneous music, delighting the Buddhas, the Bodhisattvas, and the Arhats.
At that time, their joy was beyond words.
The Buddha addressed Ānanda, the Bodhisattva Ajita, and the others, saying:
"In my description of the land of Amitābha Buddha and his bodhisattvas and arhats as being naturally composed of the seven treasures, is there perhaps any discrepancy?"
Ānanda knelt with his hands joined in reverence and said:
"The Buddha has spoken of the land of Amitābha Buddha as being joyful and excellent; it is exactly as the Buddha has described, without the slightest discrepancy."
The Buddha said:
"If I were to speak of the merits and the joyful excellence of Amitābha Buddha’s land for a full kalpa day and night, I would still not have finished.
I have merely told you this brief account."
The Bodhisattva Ajita immediately knelt with his hands joined in reverence and asked the Buddha:
"In this present Buddha-land, how many *avaivartika* bodhisattvas will there be who will be reborn in the land of Amitābha Buddha?"
"I wish to hear it.
The Buddha said,
"If you wish to know it, listen attentively and take it to heart."
The Bodhisattva Ajita replied,
"I shall receive your instruction.
The Buddha said:
"From my land, there shall be seventy-two billion *avaivartika* bodhisattvas who will all be reborn in the land of Amitābha Buddha.
Each of these *avaivartika* bodhisattvas has, throughout their past and present lives, made offerings to countless Buddhas."

Following in succession like Maitreya, they shall all become Buddhas; as for the other minor bodhisattvas, numbering in the infinite and incalculable, they shall all be reborn in the land of Amitābha Buddha.
The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Ajita:
"It is not only the bodhisattvas within my own land who shall be reborn in the land of Amitābha Buddha; there are likewise Buddhas in other lands and different realms who act in this same way."
The first Buddha is named Tathāgata Śikhin; in his land there are eighteen billion bodhisattvas, all of whom shall be reborn in the land of Amitābha Buddha.
In another distant land, the second Buddha is named Rociṣmat; in his land there are nine billion bodhisattvas, all of whom shall be reborn in the land of Amitābha Buddha.

In another land, a different country, there is a third Buddha named Zhuti Bi Hui; in that country there are twenty-two billion bodhisattvas, all of whom shall be reborn in the land of Amitābha Buddha.
In another land, a different country, there is a fourth Buddha named Amitābhasa; in that land there are twenty-five billion bodhisattvas, all of whom shall be reborn in the land of Amitābha Buddha.
In another land, a different country, there is a fifth Buddha named Lūpālipācaiye; in that country there are six billion bodhisattvas, all of whom shall be reborn in the land of Amitābha Buddha.
In another land, a different country, there is a sixth Buddha named Nayiyucai; in that country there are fourteen thousand bodhisattvas, all of whom shall be reborn in the land of Amitābha Buddha.
In another land, a foreign country, there is a seventh Buddha named Vairaprabhāsa; in that land there are fifteen bodhisattvas, all of whom shall be reborn in the Land of Amitābha Buddha.
In another land, a different country, there is an eighth Buddha named Ahecai; in that land there are eight bodhisattvas, all of whom shall be reborn in the land of Amitābha Buddha.
In another land, a foreign country, there is a ninth Buddha named Śrīguṇarāja; in that land there are eighty-one billion bodhisattvas, all of whom shall be reborn in the land of Amitābha Buddha.
In another land, a different country, there is a tenth Buddha named Natacai; in that land there are ten billion bodhisattvas, all of whom shall be reborn in the land of Amitābha Buddha.

In another land, a different country, there is an eleventh Buddha named Varanaviyucai. In that land, there are twelve thousand bodhisattvas, all of whom shall be reborn in the land of Amitābha Buddha.

In another land, a different country, there is a twelfth Buddha named P’i-t’u-yeh-ts’ai. In that land there are bodhisattvas, incalculable and beyond measure, all of whom are *avaivartika* (non-retrogressive), all possessing wisdom and valor. Each has made offerings to incalculable Buddhas, and at one time they all formed a collective aspiration to go, intending to be born in the land of Amitābha Buddha.

In another land, a different country, there is a thirteenth Buddha named Suīhēyuèzhībōduōcài; in that land there are seven hundred and ninety billion bodhisattvas, all of whom shall be reborn in the land of Amitābha Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"All these bodhisattvas are *avaivartika* (non-retrogressive).
Among the assembly of bhikṣus and the countless ranks of junior bodhisattvas, all shall be reborn in the land of Amitābha Buddha."

Not only shall the bodhisattvas from the lands of these fourteen buddhas be reborn there, but all the bodhisattvas from the countless buddha-lands of the eight directions, above, and below, each and every one of them shall likewise be reborn in the land of Amitābha Buddha.
They are exceedingly numerous; they all go together to assemble in the land of Amitābha Buddha, and the great multitude is beyond calculation.
Were I merely to recite the names of the countless Buddhas of the eight directions and the zenith and nadir, it would not be finished even in a single kalpa of day and night.

If I were to further describe the Buddha-lands of all Buddhas, the assemblies of bhikṣus, and the multitudes of bodhisattvas—enumerating the number of those who will be reborn in the land of Amitābha Buddha—I could speak for an entire kalpa without ceasing and still not reach the end.
"I have merely summarized and briefly recounted it for you all.
The Buddha said to Ānanda, the Bodhisattva Ajita, and the others:

"As for the kings, people, good sons, and good daughters of this world who, due to the merit and fortune resulting from the wholesome deeds they performed in their past lives, are now able to hear the name of Amitābha Buddha—this is most excellent and wonderful; I rejoice on their behalf."
The Buddha said:

"If there are sons of good family or daughters of good family who, upon hearing the name of Amitābha Buddha, feel joy with a compassionate heart, leaping up all at once, their minds becoming pure and the hairs on their bodies standing on end, and tears immediately falling, they have all practiced the path to Buddhahood in their past lives."

If it is because there is a Buddha in another direction, then Bodhisattvas are not ordinary people. Should there be men or women among the populace who, upon hearing the name of Amitābha Buddha, do not believe in his existence; who do not believe in the sutras or the words of the Buddha; who do not believe in the community of bhikṣus; and whose minds are filled with doubt such that they have no faith at all—these are all those who have come from the evil realms. Being ignorant and unable to understand their past lives, their calamities and evils are not yet exhausted, and they have not yet reached the point where they should be delivered. For this reason, their minds harbor doubts and they do not place their faith in him.
The Buddha said: "I tell you all:
whatever wholesome dharmas you ought to practice, you must all receive and follow them with faith, and never harbor doubt.
After I have entered parinirvāṇa, you and the people of future generations must not say again:"
"I do not believe that there is a land of Amitābha Buddha.
Therefore, I have caused you all to see the land of Amitābha Buddha; each of you should seek what it is that you ought to do.
I have fully expounded for you all the sutras, precepts, and laws of caution; you should uphold them according to the Buddha-dharma and must not let them be lost or corrupted.
I entrust this sutra to you; you should maintain it firmly and must not arbitrarily add to or subtract from the teachings of this sutra.
After my parinirvāṇa, this path of the sutras shall remain for a thousand years.

After those thousand years, the path of the sutras will be severed; out of compassion for all beings, I shall maintain and preserve these sutra teachings for another hundred years, and when those hundred years have ended, they shall finally cease and be cut off.
"Whatever one wishes for in the heart, one may all attain the Way.
The Buddha said, "The Teacher opens the ears and eyes of people; with clear and penetrating wisdom, he delivers them, enabling them to properly harmonize with the Way of Nirvana."

"One should always be filial and compassionate toward the Buddha and one's parents; one should always be mindful of the teacher’s kindness. If such mindfulness is constant and uninterrupted, one will swiftly attain the Way.
The Buddha said:
"In this world, it is extremely rare to encounter a Buddha; likewise, it is extremely rare to encounter a śramaṇa or a teacher who expounds the sutras for others."

When the Buddha preached this sutra, twelve trillion devas and humans immediately attained the divine eye of far-reaching vision, and with one mind, they all resolved to follow the path of the bodhisattvas.
Thereupon, two hundred billion devas and humans all attained the stage of Anāgāmin;
eight hundred śramaṇas all attained the stage of Arhat;
and four billion bodhisattvas all attained the stage of Avaivartika.

When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, the bodhisattvas, arhats, devas, kings, and the people were all greatly rejoiced. They rose and paid homage to the Buddha, circumambulated him three times, and then departed, bowing their heads at his feet.
The Smaller Sutra on Amitābha, Scroll II.
